name: Hydrogen

bonding.summary: Two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons: the simplest covalent bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Each atom gives its single electron to the pair, so both feel two electrons, the full first shell like helium. The atoms are identical, so they share exactly equally.

formation: Formed as the early universe cooled: H + H- -> H2 + e-
occurrence: The most abundant molecule in the universe, filling giant molecular clouds where stars form.
facts: The H2 molecule is the most common molecule in the universe.
summary: Molecular hydrogen is two protons held together by one shared pair of electrons. It is the raw material from which stars form.

name: Helium hydride ion

bonding.summary: A helium atom and a proton share two electrons, both originally helium's.
bonding.electronSharing: Helium lends its two electrons to a bond with the bare proton. They stay much closer to helium, so the positive charge sits mostly on the hydrogen end.

formation: He + H+ -> HeH+ + light (radiative association, about 100,000 years after the Big Bang)
occurrence: Thought to be the first molecule ever formed; detected in space in 2019 in the planetary nebula NGC 7027.
uses: A test case for quantum-chemistry calculations
facts: It is the strongest known acid: it would protonate almost anything.
hazards: Exists only in space or in the lab as isolated ions.
summary: HeH+ is believed to be the very first molecule in the universe, formed when the first neutral helium atoms met free protons.

name: Trihydrogen cation

structure.note: Equilateral triangle, H–H 87 pm.

bonding.summary: Three protons share just two electrons in one bond that spans the whole triangle.
bonding.electronSharing: A single electron pair is spread over all three nuclei at once, the simplest example of a three-centre two-electron bond.

occurrence: One of the most abundant ions in interstellar space; also glows in Jupiter's and Saturn's auroras.
uses: Tracing the chemistry of interstellar clouds
facts: H3+ drives most of the chemistry in cold interstellar clouds by handing protons to other molecules.
hazards: Exists only in space or plasmas.
summary: H3+ is three protons bound by two shared electrons. It kick-starts the chemistry that builds molecules between the stars.

name: Carbon monoxide

bonding.summary: A triple bond: two pairs shared normally and a third pair donated by oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon and oxygen share three electron pairs; one of them comes entirely from oxygen. Each atom keeps one lone pair. The dative pair nearly cancels oxygen's pull, so CO is only slightly polar.

formation: 2 C + O2 -> 2 CO (burning with too little oxygen)
occurrence: The second most common molecule in space after H2; on Earth from incomplete burning.
uses: Reducing iron ore in blast furnaces
Tracing star-forming gas in radio astronomy
facts: Astronomers map hydrogen clouds by the radio glow of the CO they contain.
hazards: Colorless, odorless and highly toxic: it binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen.
summary: Carbon monoxide has one of the strongest chemical bonds known. It is common in space and dangerous in homes.

name: Hydrogen cyanide

bonding.summary: A single H–C bond and a triple C≡N bond in a straight line.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon shares one pair with hydrogen and three pairs with nitrogen. Nitrogen keeps one lone pair and pulls the shared electrons toward itself.

formation: CH4 + NH3 + 3/2 O2 -> HCN + 3 H2O (Andrussow process)
occurrence: Found in comets, interstellar clouds and Titan's atmosphere; made industrially.
facts: HCN can join with itself to form adenine, a building block of DNA, which is why it interests origin-of-life researchers.
summary: Hydrogen cyanide is a small, deadly molecule that is also a likely ingredient in the chemistry that led to life.

name: Formaldehyde

bonding.summary: Carbon bonds to two hydrogens and makes a double bond to oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=O double bond shares two pairs, pulled strongly toward oxygen, which keeps two lone pairs.

formation: CH3OH -> CH2O + H2 (catalytic dehydrogenation of methanol)
occurrence: The first polyatomic organic molecule found in interstellar space (1969).
facts: Formalin, used to preserve specimens, is about 37% formaldehyde in water.
hazards: Toxic and a known human carcinogen.
summary: Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde. It is common in space and widely used to make resins.

name: Nitrogen

bonding.summary: A triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in chemistry (945 kJ/mol).
bonding.electronSharing: Each nitrogen shares three electrons, making three shared pairs, and keeps one lone pair.

formation: Separated from air by distilling liquid air
facts: Breaking the N≡N triple bond takes so much energy that the Haber process uses about 1% of the world's energy.
summary: N2's triple bond makes it so stable that most of the planet's nitrogen sits unused in the air.

name: Oxygen

bonding.summary: A double bond with two unpaired electrons.
bonding.electronSharing: In the simple picture the atoms share two pairs and each keeps two lone pairs. Molecular orbital theory shows two electrons are unpaired, which makes O2 magnetic and a 'diradical'.

occurrence: 21% of the air, made by photosynthesis.
facts: Liquid oxygen sticks between the poles of a strong magnet.
summary: O2 is the oxygen we breathe. Its two unpaired electrons make it both reactive and magnetic.

name: Ozone

bonding.summary: Two equal O–O bonds, each halfway between single and double.
bonding.electronSharing: One pair of π electrons is spread over all three atoms (resonance). The central oxygen has a lone pair, which bends the molecule.

formation: 3 O2 -> 2 O3 (ultraviolet light or electric discharge)
occurrence: The ozone layer, 15–35 km up; also ground-level smog.
facts: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV-B and UV-C light.
summary: Ozone is a three-atom form of oxygen that shields life from ultraviolet light high in the sky but harms lungs near the ground.

name: Fluorine

bonding.summary: A single bond that is unusually weak (159 kJ/mol).
bonding.electronSharing: The atoms share one pair; each keeps three lone pairs that repel each other across the short bond, weakening it.

formation: 2 HF -> H2 + F2 (electrolysis of KF in liquid HF)
occurrence: Never free in nature; made by electrolysis.
facts: The weak F–F bond plus very strong bonds to other elements make fluorine the most reactive element.
summary: F2 is the most reactive element in molecular form, held together by a surprisingly weak bond.

name: Chlorine

bonding.summary: One shared pair links two chlorine atoms.
bonding.electronSharing: Each atom contributes one electron to the pair and keeps three lone pairs, completing its octet.

formation: 2 NaCl + 2 H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2 NaOH (chlor-alkali electrolysis)
facts: About 70 million tonnes of chlorine are produced each year.
summary: Chlorine gas is made from salt water and used to disinfect water worldwide.

name: Bromine

bonding.summary: A single shared pair; strong attraction between large molecules makes it liquid.
bonding.electronSharing: One shared pair and three lone pairs on each atom. The big, soft electron clouds attract neighboring molecules.

occurrence: Extracted from brine wells and the Dead Sea.
facts: One of only two elements liquid at room temperature.
summary: Bromine is a dense red-brown liquid made of Br2 molecules.

name: Iodine

bonding.summary: A long single bond; stronger attraction between molecules makes iodine a solid.
bonding.electronSharing: One shared pair, three lone pairs on each atom.

formation: 2 I- + Cl2 -> I2 + 2 Cl- (from brines and seaweed)
occurrence: From brines, Chilean saltpeter deposits and seaweed.
facts: Iodine vapor is violet; dissolved in water with iodide it is brown.
summary: Iodine forms shiny dark crystals that turn straight into violet vapor.

name: White phosphorus

structure.note: Regular tetrahedron, P–P 221 pm.

bonding.summary: Six P–P single bonds along the edges of a tetrahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Each phosphorus shares one pair with each of the other three atoms and keeps one lone pair. The 60° angles strain the bonds.

formation: 2 Ca3(PO4)2 + 6 SiO2 + 10 C -> P4 + 6 CaSiO3 + 10 CO
occurrence: Made from phosphate rock in electric furnaces.
facts: White phosphorus glows in the dark as it slowly reacts with air (chemiluminescence).
hazards: Highly toxic; ignites spontaneously in air.
summary: P4 is a tiny, strained tetrahedron of phosphorus atoms, which makes it dangerously reactive.

name: Cyclooctasulfur

structure.note: Crown ring, S–S 205.5 pm, S–S–S 108°.

bonding.summary: Eight sulfur atoms in a puckered crown-shaped ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Each sulfur shares one pair with each ring neighbor and keeps two lone pairs.

formation: Recovered as H2S from natural gas: 2 H2S + O2 -> 2 S + 2 H2O (Claus process; S8 rings form on cooling)
occurrence: Volcanic deposits; most is recovered from natural gas and oil.
facts: Above about 160 °C the rings break open and link into long chains, so molten sulfur suddenly becomes thick.
hazards: Low toxicity; burns to toxic SO2.
summary: Ordinary yellow sulfur is a crystal of S8 crown-shaped rings.

name: Buckminsterfullerene

bonding.summary: 60 carbons each bonded to three others; 30 double bonds lie on the edges shared by two hexagons.
bonding.electronSharing: Each carbon shares pairs with three neighbors and contributes one electron to π bonding spread over the cage.

formation: Carbon vaporized by a laser or electric arc in helium condenses into C60 cages
occurrence: Found in soot, some rocks, and in space around dying stars.
facts: Its discovery in 1985 earned Kroto, Curl and Smalley the 1996 Nobel Prize.
C60 was detected in a planetary nebula in 2010; it sublimes rather than melting.
summary: C60 is a hollow sphere of carbon shaped exactly like a football, a third form of pure carbon after graphite and diamond.

name: Carbon dioxide

bonding.summary: Two C=O double bonds pointing in opposite directions.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen; oxygen pulls them closer (Δχ 0.89). Each oxygen keeps two lone pairs. The two bond dipoles cancel, so CO2 is nonpolar overall.

formation: C + O2 -> CO2; CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O (burning)
occurrence: About 0.042% of air (420 ppm in 2024) and rising.
facts: Solid CO2 sublimes at −78.5 °C at normal pressure; it is liquid only above 5.1 atm.
hazards: Asphyxiant at high concentration; main driver of climate change.
summary: CO2 is what plants breathe in and what burning releases. It traps heat in the atmosphere.

name: Nitrous oxide

bonding.summary: N–N–O in a line, with bonding between the N≡N–O and N=N=O pictures.
bonding.electronSharing: Resonance spreads the bonding pairs so the N–N bond is about 2.5 and the N–O bond about 1.5. The central nitrogen carries a partial positive charge.

occurrence: Made by soil bacteria and fertilized fields; about 0.34 ppm in air.
facts: N2O is the largest remaining ozone-depleting emission and a potent greenhouse gas.
hazards: Asphyxiant; misuse damages nerves via vitamin B12.
summary: Laughing gas is a mild anesthetic and an important greenhouse gas.

name: Nitric oxide

bonding.summary: Bond order 2.5 with one unpaired electron: a stable radical.
bonding.electronSharing: NO has 11 valence electrons, so one is left unpaired. It sits mostly on nitrogen and makes NO reactive.

formation: N2 + O2 -> 2 NO (lightning and hot engines)
occurrence: From lightning, combustion and living cells.
uses: Medical gas for lung blood vessels
facts: The discovery that NO is a signal molecule in the body won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
summary: NO is a tiny radical that pollutes city air yet also signals blood vessels to relax.

name: Nitrogen dioxide

bonding.summary: Two equal N–O bonds of order 1.5 and one unpaired electron.
bonding.electronSharing: Resonance spreads one π pair over both N–O bonds. The single unpaired electron on nitrogen bends the molecule less than a lone pair would.

occurrence: The brown haze of urban smog.
facts: Two NO2 molecules pair their lone electrons to form colorless N2O4 when cooled.
hazards: Toxic; irritates lungs and forms acid rain.
summary: NO2 is the reddish-brown gas of smog.

name: Sulfur dioxide

bonding.summary: Two strong S–O bonds and a lone pair on sulfur.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself. The lone pair on sulfur bends the molecule, so SO2 is polar.

occurrence: Volcanoes and burning sulfur-containing coal and oil.
facts: Large volcanic eruptions can cool the planet by forming sulfate haze from SO2.
summary: SO2 has a sharp smell of burnt matches and is the main cause of acid rain.

name: Sulfur trioxide

bonding.summary: Three equivalent S–O bonds in a flat triangle; no lone pair on sulfur.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur's six valence electrons all bond to oxygen; the strongly polar bonds cancel by symmetry.

formation: 2 SO2 + O2 -> 2 SO3 (vanadium pentoxide catalyst, contact process)
occurrence: Made industrially; forms in polluted air.
facts: SO3 reacts with water so violently that it is absorbed into sulfuric acid instead.
summary: SO3 is the key intermediate in making sulfuric acid.

name: Dichlorodifluoromethane (Freon-12)

bonding.summary: Carbon bonds to two chlorines and two fluorines in a tetrahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Fluorine and chlorine both pull shared electrons away from carbon. UV light high in the atmosphere breaks the weaker C–Cl bonds, releasing chlorine atoms.

occurrence: Synthetic; banned by the 1987 Montreal Protocol.
uses: Formerly refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans
facts: One chlorine atom from a CFC can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
hazards: Ozone-depleting and a powerful greenhouse gas.
summary: CFC-12 was the miracle refrigerant that turned out to tear a hole in the ozone layer.

name: Water

bonding.summary: Two polar O–H bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen but pulls them closer (Δχ 1.24), leaving O partly negative and each H partly positive. Its two lone pairs push the hydrogens together to 104.5°, and the δ+ hydrogens of one molecule cling to the lone pairs of the next: hydrogen bonds.

occurrence: Covers 71% of Earth's surface; found as ice across the Solar System.
facts: Ice floats because hydrogen bonds hold its molecules in an open lattice.
Water's boiling point would be near −80 °C without hydrogen bonding.
summary: Water is small but strongly polar, so its molecules stick together through hydrogen bonds, giving it its unusual high boiling point and floating ice.

name: Hydrogen peroxide

bonding.summary: A weak O–O single bond with an H on each oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Each oxygen shares pairs with H and the other O and keeps two lone pairs. Lone-pair repulsion makes the O–O bond weak and the molecule twisted.

formation: H2 + O2 -> H2O2 (anthraquinone process, via a catalyst)
occurrence: Made in cells and industry; in the atmosphere in small amounts.
facts: Your cells make hydrogen peroxide and destroy it with the enzyme catalase, which makes it fizz on cuts.
hazards: Concentrated solutions are corrosive and can explode with organics.
summary: H2O2 is like water with an extra oxygen; its weak O–O bond makes it a strong oxidizer and bleach.

name: Hydrogen chloride

bonding.summary: One polar H–Cl bond; in water it gives up H+ completely.
bonding.electronSharing: Chlorine pulls the shared pair toward itself (Δχ 0.96) and keeps three lone pairs. In water the bond breaks unevenly: Cl keeps both electrons as Cl−, and H+ joins water as H3O+.

occurrence: Volcanic gases and your stomach (dilute hydrochloric acid).
facts: Stomach acid is dilute hydrochloric acid; the stomach contents have a pH of about 1.5–3.5.
summary: HCl is a polar gas that becomes a strong acid in water.

name: Hydrogen fluoride

bonding.summary: The most polar single bond between two nonmetals; strong hydrogen bonding.
bonding.electronSharing: Fluorine pulls the shared pair very strongly (Δχ 1.78). The strong bond means HF releases H+ only partly in water, so it is a weak acid.

facts: HF is a weak acid yet dissolves glass, because fluoride bonds strongly to silicon.
hazards: Extremely dangerous: it penetrates skin and binds calcium in tissue.
summary: HF is a weak but very hazardous acid that can etch glass.

name: Hydrogen bromide

bonding.summary: A polar single bond, longer and weaker than H–Cl.
bonding.electronSharing: Bromine pulls the pair toward itself and keeps three lone pairs. The weaker bond makes HBr a stronger acid than HCl.

facts: Among HF, HCl, HBr and HI, acid strength rises as the bond gets longer and weaker.
summary: HBr is a strong acid in water, stronger than hydrochloric acid.

name: Hydrogen iodide

bonding.summary: The longest and weakest hydrogen-halogen bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Iodine and hydrogen pull on the pair almost equally (Δχ 0.46), but the long, weak bond breaks easily in water.

facts: HI is the strongest of the hydrohalic acids.
summary: HI is the strongest of the halogen acids because its bond is the weakest.

name: Hydrogen sulfide

bonding.summary: Like water, but with weaker polarity and almost no hydrogen bonding.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur shares one pair with each H and keeps two lone pairs. With Δχ only 0.38, the bonds are barely polar, so H2S is a gas, unlike water.

occurrence: Volcanoes, swamps, sewers and natural gas.
facts: You can smell H2S at 0.5 parts per billion, but high levels deaden the sense of smell.
hazards: Highly toxic despite its warning smell.
summary: H2S is the rotten-egg gas: water's chemical cousin, but a deadly gas.

name: Sulfuric acid

bonding.summary: Sulfur at the center of a tetrahedron of four oxygens, two carrying hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur shares electrons with four oxygens; the two O–H groups give up H+ easily because the electron-hungry SO2 group pulls electrons away from them.

occurrence: Made in larger amounts than any other chemical; also in Venus's clouds.
facts: Industrial output of sulfuric acid was once used as a measure of a country's industrial strength.
hazards: Severely corrosive; dehydrates tissue and releases great heat with water.
summary: Sulfuric acid is the world's most-produced industrial chemical.

name: Nitric acid

bonding.summary: A flat molecule: N bonded to three oxygens, one carrying the hydrogen.
bonding.electronSharing: The two terminal N–O bonds share a delocalized π pair (resonance). Nitrogen carries a formal positive charge and one oxygen a negative one.

occurrence: Synthetic; traces form from lightning in rain.
facts: Mixed with hydrochloric acid it makes aqua regia, which dissolves gold.
summary: Nitric acid is a strong oxidizing acid used mainly to make fertilizers and explosives.

name: Phosphoric acid

bonding.summary: Phosphorus in a tetrahedron of oxygens, three bearing hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: The P=O group pulls electrons away from the three O–H groups so they can release H+ one at a time.

formation: Ca5(PO4)3F + 5 H2SO4 -> 3 H3PO4 + 5 CaSO4 + HF (wet process)
facts: The tang in cola drinks comes from phosphoric acid.
summary: Phosphoric acid is a mild acid in food and a major route to fertilizers.

name: Carbonic acid

bonding.summary: A carbon bonded to one C=O and two O–H groups, all flat.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=O double bond pulls electrons and helps the O–H groups release H+. In water it falls apart into CO2 and H2O almost as fast as it forms.

occurrence: In fizzy drinks, rain and blood, always in tiny amounts.
facts: Pure carbonic acid was only isolated as a solid in 1993 and as a gas in 2011.
summary: Carbonic acid forms when CO2 dissolves in water; it makes soda tangy and buffers your blood.

name: Ammonia

bonding.summary: Three N–H bonds and one lone pair, forming a low pyramid.
bonding.electronSharing: Nitrogen shares one pair with each hydrogen and pulls them closer. Its lone pair sits on top and can grab an H+, which is why ammonia is a base.

formation: N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3 (Haber–Bosch, iron catalyst, about 450 °C and 200 atm)
occurrence: Made in huge amounts; also from decaying organic matter.
facts: Fertilizer from the Haber–Bosch process feeds roughly half of the world's population.
summary: Ammonia is the base of modern agriculture: about half the nitrogen in your body passed through a Haber–Bosch plant.

name: Sodium hydroxide (lye)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and OH− ions held by ionic attraction; the O–H inside the ion is covalent.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives its 3s electron away entirely. The hydroxide ion keeps that extra electron, shared between O and H.

formation: 2 NaCl + 2 H2O -> 2 NaOH + H2 + Cl2 (chlor-alkali process)
facts: Dissolving NaOH in water releases enough heat to make the water boil.
hazards: Severely caustic to skin and eyes.
summary: Lye is a strong base made from salt water, used to make soap and paper.

name: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ca2+ ions and two OH− ions per formula unit.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons away; each hydroxide holds one extra electron.

occurrence: Made by adding water to quicklime.
facts: Lime mortar hardens by slowly absorbing CO2 from the air and turning back into limestone.
summary: Slaked lime has been used in building mortar for thousands of years; it decomposes at 580 °C instead of melting.

name: Boric acid

bonding.summary: Boron bonded to three OH groups in a flat triangle.
bonding.electronSharing: Boron has only three valence electrons, all used in B–O bonds, leaving an empty orbital. It acts as an acid by accepting OH− from water rather than giving away H+.

facts: Its flat molecules stack in layers held by hydrogen bonds, making the crystals slippery.
hazards: Mildly toxic if swallowed in quantity.
summary: Boric acid is a weak acid that works by accepting hydroxide ions instead of releasing protons.

name: Sodium chloride (table salt)

bonding.summary: A cubic lattice of Na+ and Cl− ions, each surrounded by six of the other.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives its single outer electron to chlorine (Δχ 2.23). Na+ now has neon's electron arrangement and Cl− has argon's. The ions share nothing; they simply attract.

facts: Salt crystals are cubes because the ions stack in a cubic pattern.
A violent reaction between a soft metal and a poisonous gas gives harmless table salt.
summary: Table salt is the classic ionic compound: sodium hands an electron to chlorine and the ions lock into a cube.

name: Potassium chloride

bonding.summary: K+ and Cl− ions in the rock-salt arrangement.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium gives its 4s electron to chlorine; both ions end up with argon's electron arrangement.

occurrence: Mined from sylvite and potash deposits.
facts: About 95% of potash is used as fertilizer.
hazards: Safe in food amounts; dangerous if injected.
summary: KCl is the main potassium fertilizer and a low-sodium salt substitute.

name: Lithium fluoride

bonding.summary: Small Li+ and F− ions packed tightly in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Lithium gives its 2s electron to fluorine (Δχ 3.0), one of the most ionic bonds possible.

facts: LiF transmits ultraviolet light down to about 105 nm, further than any other common crystal.
summary: LiF is one of the most ionic compounds, valued for UV optics and radiation detectors.

name: Potassium bromide

bonding.summary: K+ and Br− ions in the rock-salt arrangement.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium transfers one electron to bromine.

uses: Pellets and windows for infrared spectroscopy
facts: In the 1800s KBr was a common sedative, the origin of the phrase 'take a bromide'.
summary: KBr is transparent to infrared light, so chemists press it into pellets to analyze samples.

name: Rubidium chloride

bonding.summary: Rb+ and Cl− ions in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Rubidium gives up its single 5s electron to chlorine.

uses: Rubidium-82 chloride for heart PET scans
Making competent bacteria in molecular biology
facts: Under pressure RbCl switches to the cesium chloride structure.
summary: RbCl is a simple salt; its radioactive form Rb-82 chloride images blood flow in the heart.

name: Silver chloride

bonding.summary: Rock-salt lattice with partly covalent bonds, which makes it insoluble in water.
bonding.electronSharing: Silver gives one electron to chlorine, but Ag+ distorts the chloride's electron cloud, so some sharing remains.

occurrence: The mineral chlorargyrite; formed in tests for chloride.
facts: Photochromic lenses darken in sunlight because AgCl crystals release silver atoms.
summary: AgCl darkens in light, the property behind early photography and self-tinting glasses.

name: Silver bromide

bonding.summary: Rock-salt lattice with partial covalent character.
bonding.electronSharing: Silver gives one electron to bromine. Light can push an electron back from Br− to Ag+, forming silver atoms: the basis of photography.

occurrence: Occurs naturally as the mineral bromargyrite; usually made synthetically.
facts: A few silver atoms formed by light make a 'latent image' that developer turns into a visible picture.
summary: AgBr is the light-sensitive heart of photographic film.

name: Magnesium oxide

bonding.summary: Doubly charged Mg2+ and O2− ions in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Magnesium gives two electrons to oxygen. The double charges make the attraction very strong, so MgO melts at 2,852 °C.

formation: 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO (the white ash of burning magnesium)
occurrence: The mineral periclase; made from magnesite or seawater.
facts: With doubly charged ions, MgO's lattice energy (about 3,800 kJ/mol) is nearly five times NaCl's.
summary: MgO is a very high-melting ionic solid that lines furnaces.

name: Calcium oxide (quicklime)

bonding.summary: Ca2+ and O2− ions in the rock-salt structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons to oxygen.

occurrence: Made in lime kilns from limestone.
facts: Heated quicklime glows brightly: the 'limelight' that lit 19th-century theaters.
hazards: Caustic; reacts with water releasing heat.
summary: Quicklime is made by baking limestone and is the starting point of cement.

name: Lead(II) sulfide (galena)

bonding.summary: Rock-salt structure, but with substantial covalent sharing; it is a semiconductor.
bonding.electronSharing: Lead and sulfur have similar electronegativities (Δχ 0.25), so electrons are shared rather than fully transferred, leaving a small band gap.

formation: Natural mineral; Pb2+ + H2S -> PbS + 2 H+
facts: Galena crystals were the first semiconductor devices, used in crystal radios around 1906.
summary: Galena is the shiny grey cubic ore of lead and an early semiconductor.

name: Cesium chloride

bonding.summary: Each large Cs+ ion sits at the center of a cube of eight Cl− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Cesium gives its 6s electron to chlorine. Because Cs+ is large it can fit eight neighbors instead of six.

facts: The Meselson–Stahl experiment of 1958 used a CsCl gradient to prove how DNA copies itself.
summary: CsCl gives its name to a crystal structure in which each ion has eight neighbors.

name: Calcium fluoride (fluorite)

bonding.summary: Ca2+ ions on a face-centered cubic lattice with F− ions filling all the tetrahedral holes.
bonding.electronSharing: Each calcium gives one electron to each of two fluorines.

occurrence: The mineral fluorite, in many colors.
uses: Lenses for UV, infrared and high-end cameras
facts: The word 'fluorescence' comes from fluorite, which glows under UV light.
summary: Fluorite gives its name to both a crystal structure and to fluorescence.

name: Zinc sulfide (sphalerite)

bonding.summary: Each Zn bonded tetrahedrally to four S, like diamond with two kinds of atoms.
bonding.electronSharing: Zinc and sulfur share electron pairs in four directional bonds, pulled toward sulfur (Δχ 0.93).

formation: Natural mineral; Zn2+ + H2S -> ZnS + 2 H+
facts: Copper-doped ZnS was the classic glow-in-the-dark material; it sublimes near 1,185 °C at normal pressure.
summary: Sphalerite names the zincblende structure used by many semiconductors.

name: Zirconium dioxide (cubic zirconia)

structure.note: Cubic form, stabilized with yttria.

bonding.summary: Zr4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure (cubic form, stabilized by yttrium).
bonding.electronSharing: Zirconium gives four electrons, two to each of two oxygens, with some covalent character.

formation: ZrSiO4 + 4 NaOH -> Na2ZrO3 + Na2SiO3 + 2 H2O (alkali fusion of zircon; the zirconate is then converted to ZrO2)
occurrence: Rare mineral baddeleyite; made from zircon.
facts: Pure ZrO2 is monoclinic; a little yttria locks it into the sparkling cubic form.
summary: Cubic zirconia is a tough, sparkling ceramic used as imitation diamond and in oxygen sensors.

name: Cerium(IV) oxide

bonding.summary: Ce4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Cerium gives four electrons to oxygen. It can easily take one back (Ce3+), releasing oxygen, which makes ceria an oxygen 'sponge'.

occurrence: Made from monazite and bastnäsite ores.
facts: Ceria is the standard powder for polishing optical glass to a flawless finish.
summary: Ceria polishes glass and helps catalytic converters by storing and releasing oxygen.

name: Thorium dioxide

bonding.summary: Th4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Thorium gives four electrons to oxygen.

occurrence: The mineral thorianite; from monazite sand.
facts: ThO2 has the highest melting point of any oxide, 3,350 °C.
summary: Thoria is the highest-melting oxide known; mixed with 1% ceria it glows brightly in lantern mantles.

name: Uranium dioxide

bonding.summary: U4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Uranium gives four electrons to oxygen, keeping two 5f electrons.

occurrence: The mineral uraninite (pitchblende); made for fuel.
uses: Nuclear fuel pellets in almost all power reactors
facts: A fuel pellet the size of a fingertip releases as much energy as about a tonne of coal.
summary: UO2 ceramic pellets are the fuel of nearly every nuclear power plant.

name: Neptunium dioxide

bonding.summary: Np4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Neptunium gives four electrons to oxygen.

uses: Target for making plutonium-238 for space batteries
facts: Irradiating NpO2 targets with neutrons makes the Pu-238 that powers deep-space probes.
summary: NpO2 is the raw material for spacecraft plutonium-238.

name: Plutonium dioxide

bonding.summary: Pu4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Plutonium gives four electrons to oxygen.

uses: Pu-238 dioxide in radioisotope generators (Voyager, Curiosity)
facts: A pellet of Pu-238 dioxide glows red-hot from its own radioactive decay.
summary: Plutonium dioxide powers spacecraft that travel too far from the Sun for solar panels.

name: Americium dioxide

bonding.summary: Am4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Americium gives four electrons to oxygen.

formation: Am2(C2O4)3 + 2 O2 -> 2 AmO2 + 6 CO2 (heating americium(III) oxalate in air)
uses: The radioactive source in ionization smoke detectors
facts: The americium in a smoke detector is AmO2 sealed between gold and silver foils.
summary: AmO2 is the tiny radioactive source inside household smoke detectors.

name: Polonium dioxide

bonding.summary: Po4+ and O2− in the fluorite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Polonium gives four electrons to oxygen.

formation: Po + O2 -> PoO2 (heating polonium in oxygen at 250 °C)
facts: It decomposes back to the elements at about 500 °C.
summary: PoO2 is a rare yellow oxide studied only in milligram amounts.

name: Uranium hexafluoride

bonding.summary: Six U–F bonds pointing to the corners of an octahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Uranium uses all six valence electrons to bond to six fluorines, which pull them strongly. The symmetric molecule is nonpolar and volatile.

facts: UF6 turns straight from solid to gas at 56.5 °C, which lets centrifuges separate U-235 from U-238 as a gas.
hazards: Radioactive; reacts with moisture to form toxic HF.
summary: UF6 is the only uranium compound volatile enough to enrich uranium as a gas.

name: Triuranium octoxide (yellowcake)
aka: yellowcake (when mixed with other uranium oxides)

structure.note: Mixed-valence oxide; real crystal is orthorhombic.

bonding.summary: A mixed-valence oxide with uranium in two oxidation states.
bonding.electronSharing: On average each uranium gives 16/3 electrons to oxygen; formally two are U5+ and one is U6+.

occurrence: The usual product of uranium mills; also in pitchblende.
facts: Despite the name, modern yellowcake is usually dark green to black; the yellow color came from older ammonium diuranate products.
summary: U3O8 is the most stable uranium oxide and the form in which uranium ore concentrate is traded.

name: Titanium dioxide (rutile)

bonding.summary: Each Ti is surrounded by an octahedron of six O; each O by a triangle of three Ti.
bonding.electronSharing: Titanium gives its four valence electrons toward oxygen, with significant covalent sharing.

uses: White pigment in paint, paper, plastics and toothpaste
facts: TiO2 has one of the highest refractive indices of any common material, which is why it is so opaque and white.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine dust is a possible carcinogen when inhaled.
summary: Titanium dioxide is the brightest white pigment, found in most paints.

name: Tin(IV) oxide (cassiterite)

bonding.summary: Rutile structure: tin octahedrally surrounded by oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Tin gives four electrons toward oxygen with partial covalent sharing.

facts: Bronze Age traders carried Cornish tin across Europe, often as smelted ingots.
summary: Cassiterite is the ore that made the Bronze Age possible.

name: Calcium titanate (perovskite)

structure.note: Idealized cubic cell; real CaTiO3 is slightly distorted (orthorhombic).

bonding.summary: Ti at the center of an oxygen octahedron, Ca in the spaces between octahedra.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons and titanium four, all ending up on the three oxygens.

occurrence: Found in the Ural Mountains in 1839; rare in crust.
uses: Gives its name to perovskite solar cells
Model for minerals deep in Earth
facts: The most abundant mineral in Earth's lower mantle, bridgmanite, has the perovskite structure.
summary: Perovskite gives its name to one of the most important crystal structures in materials science.

name: Strontium titanate

bonding.summary: The textbook cubic perovskite.
bonding.electronSharing: Strontium gives two electrons and titanium four to the oxygens.

facts: Lightly electron-doped SrTiO3 becomes a superconductor below about 0.3 K.
summary: SrTiO3 is the classic cubic perovskite crystal.

name: Barium titanate

structure.note: Cubic form above 120 °C; slightly tetragonal at room temperature.

bonding.summary: A perovskite in which the Ti ion shifts slightly off-center, creating permanent electric dipoles.
bonding.electronSharing: Barium gives two and titanium four electrons to oxygen; the off-center Ti makes the crystal ferroelectric.

uses: Multilayer ceramic capacitors (billions made each year)
facts: Every smartphone contains hundreds of tiny BaTiO3 capacitors.
summary: Barium titanate's shifting titanium ions make it ferroelectric, perfect for capacitors.

name: Iridium(IV) oxide

bonding.summary: Rutile structure, but metallic: its partly filled 5d band conducts electricity.
bonding.electronSharing: Iridium gives four electrons toward oxygen; its remaining 5d electrons are shared through the crystal like a metal.

formation: Ir + O2 -> IrO2 (heating iridium in air)
uses: Anode catalyst for splitting water in PEM electrolyzers
facts: IrO2 is one of the few catalysts that survive the harsh acid of green-hydrogen electrolyzers; it decomposes near 1,100 °C.
summary: IrO2 is a conductive oxide that catalyzes oxygen release in green-hydrogen production.

name: Calcium carbonate (calcite, chalk)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ca2+ ions attract flat carbonate ions; inside carbonate, C and O share electrons.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium hands two electrons to the carbonate group. Within CO3 2−, carbon's bonds to three oxygens are equal, each about 1⅓ bonds, because a π pair is spread over all three (resonance).

formation: Ca2+ + CO3 2- -> CaCO3 (shells, coral, cave formations); CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3
occurrence: Limestone, marble, chalk, seashells, coral reefs, stalactites.
facts: A clear calcite crystal splits light in two, showing a double image (birefringence).
It decomposes to lime and CO2 near 825 °C instead of melting.
summary: Calcium carbonate builds shells, coral and whole mountains of limestone.

name: Calcium sulfate dihydrate (gypsum)

structure.note: One formula unit with its two waters of crystallization.

bonding.summary: Ca2+ and SO4 2− ions with water molecules locked into the crystal.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons to the sulfate group. Water molecules bind to calcium through oxygen lone pairs and hydrogen-bond to sulfate.

occurrence: Evaporite beds; giant crystals in Mexico's Naica cave.
facts: Heating gypsum to about 150 °C drives off water to make plaster of Paris, which sets hard when wetted.
The Naica caves hold gypsum crystals over 11 m long.
summary: Gypsum is the soft mineral in drywall and plaster casts.

name: Barium sulfate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ba2+ and SO4 2− ions packed so tightly that water can barely separate them.
bonding.electronSharing: Barium gives two electrons to the sulfate group, whose four S–O bonds share the extra charge equally.

facts: It is safe to swallow because almost none of it dissolves, even in stomach acid.
hazards: Insoluble and safe; soluble barium salts are toxic.
summary: Barium sulfate is dense, insoluble and opaque to X-rays.

name: Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate (Epsom salt)

structure.note: One formula unit; in the crystal six waters surround each Mg2+.

bonding.summary: Mg2+ ions wrapped in six water molecules, plus sulfate and one more water.
bonding.electronSharing: Magnesium gives two electrons to sulfate; water oxygens donate lone pairs toward Mg2+.

occurrence: Named after a bitter spring at Epsom, England.
facts: Magnesium sulfate is one of the main salts in seawater after sodium chloride.
summary: Epsom salt is a hydrated magnesium salt used in baths, farming and medicine.

name: Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate

structure.note: One formula unit; four waters bind directly to copper.

bonding.summary: Cu2+ ions surrounded by water molecules that donate lone pairs; sulfate balances the charge.
bonding.electronSharing: Water oxygens donate lone pairs into empty copper orbitals (coordinate bonds). Light absorbed by copper's d electrons gives the deep blue color.

uses: Testing for water (white anhydrous salt turns blue)
facts: Heating the blue crystals drives off the water, leaving a white powder that turns blue again when wet.
hazards: Harmful if swallowed; toxic to fish.
summary: Blue vitriol is a beautiful example of how water bound to metal ions creates color.

name: Potassium nitrate (saltpeter)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: K+ ions and flat nitrate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium gives one electron to the nitrate group, whose three N–O bonds share a delocalized π pair.

occurrence: Cave and desert deposits; once scraped from manure heaps.
facts: Gunpowder burns because nitrate supplies its own oxygen; it decomposes above 400 °C.
summary: Saltpeter is the oxygen supplier in gunpowder and a valuable fertilizer.

name: Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and hydrogen carbonate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives an electron to the HCO3 group, where the extra charge is shared by the two oxygens without hydrogen.

formation: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl (Solvay process)
occurrence: The mineral nahcolite; mostly made by the Solvay process.
facts: Above about 50 °C it breaks down: 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, which makes cakes rise.
summary: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated or mixed with acid.

name: Sodium carbonate (washing soda)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Two Na+ ions for each carbonate ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each sodium gives one electron; carbonate shares the two extra electrons over its three oxygens.

occurrence: Trona deposits and the Solvay process.
facts: Ancient Egyptians used natural soda (natron) to mummify bodies.
summary: Soda ash is a key ingredient of ordinary glass.

name: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and hypochlorite ions with a Cl–O single bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium's electron ends up mostly on the oxygen of ClO−; chlorine is in the unusual +1 oxidation state, which makes it a strong oxidizer.

facts: Mixing bleach with acids releases chlorine gas; mixing it with ammonia releases toxic chloramines.
hazards: Corrosive; never mix with acids or ammonia.
summary: Household bleach is a dilute solution of sodium hypochlorite.

name: Lithium carbonate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Two Li+ ions with one carbonate ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each lithium gives up its 2s electron to the carbonate group.

formation: 2 LiCl + Na2CO3 -> Li2CO3 + 2 NaCl (from salt-flat brines)
occurrence: Made from brines in salt flats and from spodumene ore.
facts: Its use for bipolar disorder was discovered by John Cade in 1949.
hazards: Toxic in overdose; doses must be monitored.
summary: Lithium carbonate is both a battery raw material and a psychiatric medicine.

name: Strontium nitrate (red fireworks)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Sr2+ ions and two nitrate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Strontium gives one electron to each nitrate. In a flame, excited strontium species emit red light.

facts: The red of fireworks comes mainly from SrOH and SrCl formed in the flame.
summary: Strontium nitrate makes the brilliant red in fireworks.

name: Potassium permanganate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: K+ ions and tetrahedral permanganate ions with Mn in its highest state, +7.
bonding.electronSharing: Manganese has given all seven valence electrons toward oxygen. Light pushes electrons from oxygen back toward manganese, which absorbs green-yellow light and makes the deep purple color.

formation: 2 MnO2 + 4 KOH + O2 -> 2 K2MnO4 + 2 H2O; then oxidized to KMnO4
facts: A few crystals turn a whole bucket of water purple; it decomposes at about 240 °C.
summary: Potassium permanganate is a vivid purple oxidizer used to clean water.

name: Potassium dichromate

structure.note: Two CrO4 tetrahedra sharing one oxygen, Cr–O–Cr 126°.

bonding.summary: Two chromium-oxygen tetrahedra joined through a shared oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Each chromium (+6) has given its six valence electrons toward oxygen. Charge transfer from oxygen to chromium absorbs blue light, giving the orange color.

uses: Old breathalyzers (orange turns green with alcohol)
facts: Early breathalyzers measured alcohol by how much orange dichromate turned green.
summary: Bright orange dichromate is a powerful oxidizer and a classic, but hazardous, lab reagent.

name: Thallium(I) sulfate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Two Tl+ ions with one sulfate.
bonding.electronSharing: Each thallium gives one 6p electron and keeps its 6s pair (inert pair effect).

uses: Formerly rat poison and insecticide (banned in many countries)
facts: The body mistakes Tl+ for K+, which is what makes it so poisonous.
summary: Thallium sulfate was a notorious poison because thallium imitates potassium.

name: Radium chloride

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ra2+ ions and Cl− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Radium gives its two 7s electrons, one to each chlorine.

formation: RaCO3 + 2 HCl -> RaCl2 + CO2 + H2O (Curie turned radium-bearing sulfates into carbonates, dissolved them in HCl, then purified the chloride by fractional crystallization)
uses: Radium-223 dichloride treats prostate cancer that has spread to bone
facts: Marie Curie first isolated radium as its chloride in 1902; it glows blue-green in the dark.
summary: Radium chloride was the first radium compound purified and is now a cancer drug.

name: Sodium pertechnetate (Tc-99m imaging agent)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ and the tetrahedral pertechnetate ion, Tc in the +7 state.
bonding.electronSharing: Technetium shares all seven valence electrons with four oxygens; the ion carries one extra electron from sodium.

formation: 99MoO4 2- -> 99mTcO4- + e- (beta decay of molybdate in a generator; eluted with saline as NaTcO4)
uses: Thyroid, brain and other diagnostic scans
Starting material for most Tc-99m imaging kits
facts: Tc-99m is used in tens of millions of scans per year because its 6-hour half-life and gentle gamma rays are ideal for imaging.
summary: Pertechnetate solutions deliver the world's most used medical isotope.

name: Promethium(III) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Pm3+ ions and three Cl− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Promethium gives three electrons, like all lanthanides.

occurrence: Made in tiny amounts from reactor fission products.
uses: Research; promethium salts were once used in luminous paint
facts: Promethium salts glow pale blue-green from their own radioactivity.
summary: Promethium chloride is a rare glowing salt of the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes.

name: Rhodium(III) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit; the real solid is a layered network.

bonding.summary: Rh3+ surrounded octahedrally by chloride in a layered crystal.
bonding.electronSharing: Rhodium gives three electrons to chlorine with substantial covalent sharing.

uses: Starting material for rhodium catalysts such as Wilkinson's catalyst
facts: The red hydrate RhCl3·3H2O is the usual entry point to rhodium chemistry; the anhydrous salt decomposes above about 450 °C.
summary: RhCl3 is the gateway compound for making rhodium catalysts.

name: Palladium(II) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit; the real solid is made of square-planar chains.

bonding.summary: Pd2+ bonded to four bridging chlorides in square-planar chains.
bonding.electronSharing: Palladium shares electrons with chlorides in a square-planar arrangement typical of d8 ions.

facts: Palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling earned the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
summary: PdCl2 is the starting point for many of chemistry's most important catalysts.

name: Cobalt(II) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Co2+ and Cl− ions; with water, Co2+ binds six water molecules.
bonding.electronSharing: Cobalt gives two electrons to chlorine. In the hydrate, water lone pairs bond to Co2+ and shift its d-electron energies, changing the color from blue to pink.

uses: Humidity indicator in silica gel (blue dry, pink wet)
facts: Dry blue CoCl2 turns pink as it absorbs water, forming the hydrate CoCl2·6H2O.
summary: Cobalt chloride changes from blue to pink with moisture, so it signals humidity.

name: Iron(III) oxide (hematite, rust)

structure.note: One formula unit; real hematite has the corundum structure.

bonding.summary: Fe3+ and O2− ions in the corundum-type structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Each iron gives three electrons toward oxygen; light absorbed by iron's d electrons gives the red-brown color.

formation: 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3 (rusting needs water too)
occurrence: The main iron ore; red soil and the surface of Mars.
facts: Mars is red because its dust is rich in iron oxides.
summary: Hematite is the most important iron ore and the red in rust, ochre and Mars.

name: Iron(II,III) oxide (magnetite)

structure.note: One formula unit; the real crystal is an inverse spinel.

bonding.summary: One Fe2+ and two Fe3+ per four oxide ions, in an inverse spinel structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Electrons hop between Fe2+ and Fe3+ sites, so magnetite conducts electricity; the iron spins align into strong magnetism.

formation: 3 Fe + 4 H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4 H2 (hot iron and steam)
occurrence: Common in igneous rocks and black sands.
facts: Natural lodestones of magnetite were the first compasses.
Some bacteria use magnetite crystals to sense Earth's magnetic field, and some animals may too.
summary: Magnetite is the most magnetic natural mineral, used in the first compasses.

name: Iron disulfide (pyrite, fool's gold)

structure.note: One formula unit; the real crystal arranges these like NaCl.

bonding.summary: Fe2+ ions and S2 2− 'persulfide' pairs, arranged like a stretched rock-salt lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Iron gives two electrons to an S–S pair; the two sulfurs share one pair between them, like the O–O bond in peroxide.

formation: Fe2+ + 2 HS- -> FeS2 + H2 (in oxygen-poor sediments)
uses: Source of sulfur and sulfuric acid
facts: Its name comes from Greek pyr, fire, because it sparks when struck.
hazards: Weathering releases sulfuric acid (acid mine drainage).
summary: Pyrite's brassy cubes have fooled gold prospectors for centuries.

name: Aluminium oxide (corundum, ruby, sapphire)

structure.note: One formula unit; real corundum has hexagonal close-packed oxide with Al in octahedral holes.

bonding.summary: Small, highly charged Al3+ ions in octahedral holes between close-packed O2− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Each aluminium gives three electrons toward oxygen; the bonds are strong and partly covalent, making corundum extremely hard.

formation: 2 Al(OH)3 -> Al2O3 + 3 H2O (Bayer process from bauxite)
occurrence: Bauxite ore; gem corundum in metamorphic rocks.
facts: Ruby is corundum with traces of chromium; blue sapphire contains iron and titanium.
Corundum is 9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond among common minerals.
summary: Alumina is the raw material for aluminium and, as corundum, the gems ruby and sapphire.

name: Chromium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; corundum structure.

bonding.summary: Cr3+ in octahedral holes between oxide ions (corundum structure).
bonding.electronSharing: Chromium gives three electrons toward oxygen; its three remaining d electrons absorb red light, so it looks green.

facts: The green on many banknotes and in camouflage paint uses chromium oxide pigments.
summary: Chromium oxide is a durable green pigment.

name: Manganese dioxide (pyrolusite)

bonding.summary: Mn4+ in oxygen octahedra, in the rutile structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Manganese gives four electrons toward oxygen and readily accepts some back, which makes MnO2 a good battery cathode.

uses: Cathode of alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries
facts: Neanderthals used manganese dioxide as black pigment and possibly to start fires.
It decomposes to Mn2O3 and oxygen above 535 °C.
summary: MnO2 powers ordinary alkaline batteries.

name: Mercury(II) sulfide (cinnabar)

structure.note: One formula unit; the real red form has helical Hg–S chains.

bonding.summary: Spiral chains of alternating Hg and S atoms.
bonding.electronSharing: Mercury and sulfur share electron pairs (Δχ 0.58) along the chains; the band gap absorbs blue-green light, giving the scarlet color.

occurrence: Hydrothermal veins; the main mercury ore (e.g. Almadén, Spain).
facts: Vermilion paint from cinnabar colored Roman frescoes and Chinese lacquerware; it sublimes near 580 °C.
summary: Cinnabar is the scarlet ore of mercury and the source of vermilion pigment.

name: Silicon dioxide (quartz, shown as cristobalite network)

structure.note: Idealized beta-cristobalite; quartz links the same SiO4 tetrahedra in spirals.

bonding.summary: A 3D network of SiO4 tetrahedra, each oxygen bridging two silicons.
bonding.electronSharing: Each silicon shares one pair with each of four oxygens, and each oxygen bonds to two silicons, keeping two lone pairs. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons (Δχ 1.54).

formation: Si + O2 -> SiO2; natural crystallization from magma and hot water
occurrence: One of the most common minerals in Earth's crust: quartz, sand, flint, opal.
uses: Quartz crystal oscillators in clocks and phones
facts: Quartz vibrates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied, keeping time in watches.
hazards: Breathing fine crystalline silica dust causes silicosis.
summary: Silica is a giant covalent network: no separate molecules, just endless Si–O–Si links.

name: Arsenic trioxide

bonding.summary: Molecules of As4O6: four arsenic atoms bridged by six oxygens in a cage.
bonding.electronSharing: Each arsenic shares pairs with three oxygens and keeps one lone pair; each oxygen bridges two arsenic atoms.

occurrence: By-product of copper and gold smelting; mineral arsenolite.
facts: Once called 'inheritance powder', it is now an approved leukemia drug.
summary: Arsenic trioxide went from infamous poison to life-saving leukemia medicine.

name: Antimony trisulfide (stibnite)

structure.note: One formula unit; real stibnite has ribbon-like chains.

bonding.summary: Ribbons of Sb–S bonds; antimony and sulfur share electrons fairly evenly.
bonding.electronSharing: Antimony shares electrons with sulfur (Δχ 0.53) and keeps a lone pair that shapes the ribbons.

occurrence: The main antimony ore, often in long needle crystals.
facts: Stibnite forms spectacular metallic needles up to tens of centimeters long.
summary: Stibnite is the needle-shaped ore of antimony.

name: Vanadium pentoxide

structure.note: One formula unit; the real solid is layered.

bonding.summary: Layers of VO5 square pyramids with a short V=O bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Vanadium has given all five valence electrons toward oxygen and can take one back easily, which makes it a good oxidation catalyst.

occurrence: From vanadium ores and oil residues.
facts: V2O5 converts SO2 to SO3 in the contact process, making most of the world's sulfuric acid.
summary: Vanadium pentoxide is the catalyst behind sulfuric acid production.

name: Tungsten carbide

bonding.summary: Carbon atoms sit in trigonal prisms of tungsten atoms; bonding mixes covalent and metallic character.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon shares electrons with six tungsten neighbors, while tungsten's d electrons stay partly delocalized, so WC conducts electricity.

occurrence: Almost all synthetic; it also occurs as the very rare natural mineral qusongite.
facts: Tungsten carbide is roughly three times as stiff as steel.
hazards: Dust is harmful to lungs (especially with cobalt binder).
summary: Tungsten carbide is one of the hardest practical materials, used for cutting tools.

name: Molybdenum disulfide (molybdenite)

bonding.summary: Sandwich layers S–Mo–S held to each other only by weak forces.
bonding.electronSharing: Within a layer, molybdenum shares electrons with six sulfurs in a trigonal prism. Between layers there are no bonds, so they slide easily.

uses: Catalyst for removing sulfur from fuels
facts: A single layer of MoS2 is a semiconductor only three atoms thick.
summary: MoS2 is a slippery layered mineral, like graphite, used as a lubricant.

name: Bismuth telluride

structure.note: Charges are formal; the real crystal is layered Te–Bi–Te–Bi–Te.

bonding.summary: Five-atom layers Te–Bi–Te–Bi–Te stacked with weak links between them.
bonding.electronSharing: Bismuth and tellurium share electrons almost equally (Δχ 0.08), giving a narrow band gap.

facts: Its surface conducts electricity even though its interior does not: it is a topological insulator.
summary: Bismuth telluride turns heat into electricity and powers Peltier coolers.

name: Scandium oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real crystal is the cubic bixbyite type.

bonding.summary: Sc3+ and O2− ions in the cubic bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Each scandium gives all three valence electrons to oxygen.

occurrence: Recovered from uranium, titanium and rare-earth processing.
uses: Electrolytes for solid oxide fuel cells
facts: World scandium supply is only tens of tonnes a year.
summary: Scandia is a very high-melting oxide that feeds scandium alloys and fuel cells.

name: Yttrium oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; bixbyite structure.

bonding.summary: Y3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Yttrium gives three electrons to oxygen.

facts: Europium-doped yttria made the red dots in color TV screens.
summary: Yttria is the host crystal for many phosphors and stabilizes zirconia.

name: Lanthanum oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real crystal is hexagonal (A-type).

bonding.summary: Large La3+ ions with seven oxygen neighbors.
bonding.electronSharing: Lanthanum gives three electrons to oxygen.

uses: High-refractive optical glass for camera lenses
facts: Many high-end camera lenses contain glass that is up to 40% lanthanum oxide.
summary: Lanthanum oxide gives optical glass a high refractive index.

name: Praseodymium(III,IV) oxide

structure.note: Mixed-valence, fluorite-related structure.

bonding.summary: A mixed-valence oxide: four Pr4+ and two Pr3+ per eleven oxygens.
bonding.electronSharing: Most praseodymium atoms give four electrons, some three, so oxygen vacancies form in a fluorite-like lattice.

formation: Heating praseodymium salts in air above about 500 °C
facts: It is the stable dark-brown oxide that forms when praseodymium burns in air.
summary: Pr6O11 is a mixed-valence oxide behind the bright yellow of many ceramic glazes.

name: Europium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Eu3+ and O2− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Europium gives three electrons. Its remaining 4f electrons jump between levels and emit sharp red light.

uses: Red phosphors for screens and lamps
facts: Europium's red glow has an unusually narrow color band, which is ideal for displays.
summary: Europium oxide is the source of the pure red glow in displays.

name: Gadolinium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Gd3+ and O2− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Gadolinium gives three electrons and keeps a half-filled 4f7 shell with seven unpaired electrons.

uses: Burnable neutron absorber mixed into nuclear fuel
facts: Adding Gd2O3 to fuel pellets evens out reactor power early in a fuel cycle.
summary: Gadolinia soaks up neutrons inside nuclear fuel.

name: Holmium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ho3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Holmium gives three electrons; its 4f electrons absorb light at very sharp, well-known wavelengths.

uses: Yellow and red colorant for glass and cubic zirconia
facts: Holmium oxide looks tan in daylight but pink under fluorescent light.
summary: Holmia's sharp absorption lines make it a calibration standard.

name: Erbium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Er3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Erbium gives three electrons; its 4f electrons absorb green light, so the oxide is pink.

uses: Pink colorant for glass and porcelain
facts: Erbium-colored glass is used in some sunglasses and cheap jewelry for its pink tint.
summary: Erbia is a pink oxide that colors glass.

name: Thulium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Tm3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Thulium gives three electrons to oxygen.

uses: Target for making thulium-170 X-ray sources
facts: Irradiated thulium oxide makes portable X-ray sources that need no electricity.
summary: Thulia is the precursor to portable thulium-170 X-ray sources.

name: Ytterbium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Yb3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Ytterbium gives three electrons to oxygen.

facts: Ytterbium-doped fiber lasers are among the most efficient high-power lasers.
summary: Ytterbia is the raw material for ytterbium laser crystals and fibers.

name: Lutetium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Lu3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Lutetium gives three electrons, leaving a full 4f14 shell.

uses: Making LYSO scintillator crystals for PET scanners
facts: Lutetium-based crystals detect the gamma rays in most modern PET scanners.
summary: Lutetia is the basis of the scintillator crystals in PET scanners.

name: Hafnium dioxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real hafnia is monoclinic like zirconia.

bonding.summary: Hf4+ and O2− in a monoclinic structure, like zirconia.
bonding.electronSharing: Hafnium gives four electrons toward oxygen; the highly polarizable bonds give it a high dielectric constant.

formation: HfCl4 + 2 H2O -> HfO2 + 4 HCl (atomic layer deposition)
uses: High-k gate insulator in modern transistors
facts: Since 2007, hafnium oxide has replaced silicon dioxide as the gate insulator in leading-edge chips.
summary: Hafnia insulating layers only a few nanometers thick made modern transistors possible.

name: Tantalum pentoxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real solid has complex chains of TaO6/TaO7 polyhedra.

bonding.summary: Ta5+ in oxygen polyhedra; highly insulating with a high dielectric constant.
bonding.electronSharing: Tantalum gives all five valence electrons toward oxygen.

facts: The thin oxide grown on tantalum powder is what stores charge in a tantalum capacitor.
summary: Ta2O5 is the insulating film inside tantalum capacitors.

name: Rhenium(VII) oxide

structure.note: Formal charges; the gas is O3Re–O–ReO3 molecules and the solid a polymer of linked ReO4 and ReO6 units.

bonding.summary: In the gas, two ReO4 tetrahedra share one oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Rhenium shares all seven valence electrons with oxygen in strong, largely covalent bonds.

uses: Making perrhenic acid and rhenium catalysts
facts: It sublimes at about 360 °C, so it can be purified by vapor transport.
summary: Re2O7 is a volatile yellow oxide used to make rhenium catalysts.

name: Silicon carbide

structure.note: Cubic 3C-SiC; many other stacking forms exist.

bonding.summary: Every Si bonded to four C and every C to four Si: a diamond-like network of two elements.
bonding.electronSharing: Silicon and carbon share electron pairs in four tetrahedral bonds, pulled toward carbon (Δχ 0.65).

formation: SiO2 + 3 C -> SiC + 2 CO (Acheson process, about 2,500 °C)
occurrence: Rare natural mineral moissanite; found in meteorites as grains older than the Sun.
facts: Some SiC grains in meteorites formed around stars that died before the Sun was born.
summary: Silicon carbide is a hard semiconductor that handles high voltages in electric vehicles.

name: Gallium arsenide

bonding.summary: Ga and As each bonded to four of the other in a zincblende lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Gallium brings three valence electrons and arsenic five; together they make four shared pairs per atom (Δχ 0.37).

formation: Ga + As -> GaAs (grown as single crystals)
facts: Electrons move about five times faster in GaAs than in silicon.
summary: GaAs is a fast semiconductor used in phones and space solar panels.

name: Gallium nitride

bonding.summary: Each Ga bonded to four N in a hexagonal wurtzite lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Gallium and nitrogen share pairs strongly pulled toward nitrogen (Δχ 1.23), giving a wide band gap that emits blue light.

facts: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics honored the invention of efficient blue GaN LEDs.
summary: GaN made blue LEDs, and therefore white LED lighting, possible.

name: Indium phosphide

bonding.summary: Zincblende lattice of In and P.
bonding.electronSharing: Indium's three and phosphorus's five valence electrons form four shared pairs per atom.

uses: Lasers and detectors for fiber-optic communication
facts: InP lasers emit at 1.3 and 1.55 µm, the wavelengths that travel farthest in glass fiber.
summary: InP lasers send light down the internet's fiber-optic cables.

name: Cadmium telluride

bonding.summary: Zincblende lattice of Cd and Te.
bonding.electronSharing: Cadmium and tellurium share pairs fairly evenly (Δχ 0.41); the band gap of 1.5 eV suits sunlight.

facts: CdTe panels are the second most common solar technology after silicon.
summary: CdTe thin films make low-cost solar panels.

name: Cadmium sulfide

bonding.summary: Wurtzite lattice of Cd and S.
bonding.electronSharing: Cadmium and sulfur share pairs pulled toward sulfur (Δχ 0.89); the 2.4 eV band gap absorbs blue light, so CdS is yellow.

uses: Buffer layer in thin-film solar cells
facts: Painters such as Monet used cadmium yellow.
summary: CdS is a bright yellow pigment and light-sensitive semiconductor.

name: Zinc oxide

bonding.summary: Each Zn tetrahedrally bonded to four O in wurtzite.
bonding.electronSharing: Zinc gives its two 4s electrons toward oxygen with strong polarity (Δχ 1.79).

uses: Varistors that protect electronics from surges
facts: ZnO is white at room temperature but turns yellow when hot.
hazards: Low toxicity; fumes cause metal fume fever.
summary: Zinc oxide protects skin from UV and helps make car tires.

name: Indium tin oxide

structure.note: Host In2O3 formula unit; about 10% of indium is replaced by tin (Sn4+), each releasing a free electron.

bonding.summary: An In2O3 lattice in which Sn4+ replaces some In3+.
bonding.electronSharing: Each Sn4+ that replaces In3+ gives one extra electron to the crystal, making it conduct like a metal while staying transparent.

formation: Sputtering In2O3 and SnO2 targets onto glass
facts: Almost every touchscreen has a layer of ITO only about 100 nm thick.
summary: ITO is a transparent conductor, the invisible wiring of touchscreens.

name: Yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO)

structure.note: Formal charges; the real crystal is a layered perovskite with CuO2 planes and CuO chains.

bonding.summary: Layers of CuO2 planes separated by Y, Ba and CuO chains.
bonding.electronSharing: Copper and oxygen share electrons in flat CuO2 sheets. Missing electrons ('holes') in those sheets pair up below 93 K and flow with zero resistance.

formation: Y2O3 + 4 BaCO3 + 6 CuO + 1/2 O2 -> 2 YBa2Cu3O7 + 4 CO2 (sintered at about 950 °C in oxygen)
facts: Discovered in 1987, it was the first superconductor above the 77 K boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
summary: YBCO superconducts at 93 K, warm enough to cool with cheap liquid nitrogen.

name: Lithium cobalt oxide

structure.note: Real structure: layers of CoO2 with lithium ions between them.

bonding.summary: Layers of CoO2 sheets with Li+ ions in between that can slide in and out.
bonding.electronSharing: When the battery charges, Li+ leaves the layers and cobalt gives up an electron (Co3+ to Co4+); discharging reverses it.

uses: Cathode of lithium-ion batteries in phones and laptops
facts: John Goodenough's 1980 discovery of LiCoO2 cathodes contributed to his 2019 Nobel Prize.
hazards: Toxic; can release oxygen if overheated.
summary: LiCoO2 is the cathode in most phone and laptop batteries.

name: Boron trifluoride

bonding.summary: Boron bonded to three fluorines in a flat triangle, with an empty orbital.
bonding.electronSharing: Boron shares its three electrons with three fluorines, leaving only six electrons around it. Its empty p orbital eagerly accepts a lone pair from other molecules (a Lewis acid).

formation: B2O3 + 3 CaF2 + 3 H2SO4 -> 2 BF3 + 3 CaSO4 + 3 H2O
uses: Catalyst in organic chemistry and polymerization
facts: BF3 is the textbook example of a molecule with an incomplete octet.
summary: BF3 is electron-poor boron's classic molecule, hungry for a lone pair.

name: Beryllium chloride (gas-phase monomer)

bonding.summary: In the gas, a straight Cl–Be–Cl molecule; in the solid, chains of bridged BeCl4 tetrahedra.
bonding.electronSharing: Beryllium shares its two electrons with two chlorines, ending with just four electrons around it, so it pulls in extra chlorine lone pairs when it can.

facts: BeCl2 is a standard example of a linear molecule in VSEPR theory.
hazards: Toxic; beryllium compounds cause lung disease.
summary: Gas-phase BeCl2 is a perfectly linear molecule with an electron-poor center.

name: Diborane

structure.note: B–H terminal 119 pm, B–H bridging 133 pm.

bonding.summary: Four normal B–H bonds plus two 'banana' bridges where one H holds both borons.
bonding.electronSharing: Boron lacks electrons, so each bridging hydrogen shares a single pair between two borons: a three-centre two-electron bond. Thin lines show the two halves of each bridge.
bonding.geometry: Two BH2 groups linked by two bridging H
bonding.bondLengths: B–H(terminal) 119 pm, B–H(bridge) 133 pm, B···B 177 pm

uses: Making boron compounds and reducing agents
facts: Explaining diborane's bridges helped William Lipscomb win the 1976 Nobel Prize.
summary: Diborane's bridging hydrogens showed chemists that a bond can link three atoms.

name: Silane

bonding.summary: Silicon's analogue of methane.
bonding.electronSharing: Silicon shares one pair with each of four hydrogens. Hydrogen is slightly more electronegative (2.20 vs 1.90), so the electrons lean toward H, the reverse of methane.

uses: Depositing silicon films in chips and solar cells
facts: Silane ignites spontaneously in air.
summary: Silane is silicon's version of methane and a source of pure silicon films.

name: Silicon tetrachloride

bonding.summary: Silicon tetrahedrally bonded to four chlorines.
bonding.electronSharing: Silicon shares a pair with each chlorine; chlorine pulls them toward itself (Δχ 1.26).

facts: It fumes in moist air, reacting with water to form silica and HCl.
summary: SiCl4 is a route to the purest silicon and glass for optical fiber.

name: Germane

bonding.summary: Germanium tetrahedrally bonded to four hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: Germanium shares one pair with each H; the polarity is small (Δχ 0.19).

facts: Germane was detected in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn.
summary: Germane is germanium's methane, used to grow semiconductor films.

name: Arsine

bonding.summary: A pyramid like ammonia, but much flatter at the top.
bonding.electronSharing: Arsenic shares one pair with each H and keeps a lone pair in an s-rich orbital, so the H–As–H angle is only 92°.

facts: The Marsh test for arsenic poisoning (1836) turned arsenic into arsine and caught it as a mirror on glass.
summary: Arsine is a deadly gas vital to the semiconductor industry.

name: Hydrogen selenide

bonding.summary: A bent molecule like H2S with an even smaller angle.
bonding.electronSharing: Selenium shares one pair with each H and keeps two lone pairs; Δχ is 0.35.

uses: Making selenium semiconductors and solar cells
facts: It is more acidic than H2S because the H–Se bond is weaker.
summary: H2Se is the selenium cousin of water and hydrogen sulfide.

name: Phosphine

bonding.summary: A pyramid with a lone pair on phosphorus.
bonding.electronSharing: Phosphorus and hydrogen have almost the same electronegativity (2.19 vs 2.20), so the pairs are shared evenly.

occurrence: Found in Jupiter and Saturn; traces from anaerobic decay.
facts: A 2020 claim of phosphine in Venus's clouds sparked debate about possible life there.
summary: Phosphine is a toxic gas and a debated biosignature on Venus.

name: Phosphorus trichloride

bonding.summary: Phosphorus bonded to three chlorines with a lone pair on top.
bonding.electronSharing: Phosphorus shares one pair with each chlorine (Δχ 0.97) and keeps one lone pair.

uses: Making herbicides (glyphosate), insecticides and flame retardants
facts: It is one of the most important phosphorus intermediates, made in over a million tonnes a year.
summary: PCl3 is the gateway to most organophosphorus chemicals.

name: Phosphorus pentachloride

bonding.summary: Five P–Cl bonds: three around the middle and two longer ones at the poles.
bonding.electronSharing: Phosphorus uses all five valence electrons to bond to five chlorines, going beyond an octet; the axial bonds are longer and weaker.

facts: In the solid it rearranges into ions: [PCl4]+ [PCl6]−.
summary: PCl5 is the classic trigonal bipyramidal molecule.

name: Phosphorus pentoxide

bonding.summary: A P4O6 cage with one extra oxygen sticking out from each phosphorus.
bonding.electronSharing: Each phosphorus shares pairs with three bridging oxygens and makes a short P=O bond to a terminal oxygen.

facts: It grabs water so strongly it can pull H2O out of sulfuric and nitric acids.
summary: P4O10 is a cage molecule and one of the strongest drying agents known.

name: Sulfur hexafluoride

bonding.summary: Six fluorines around sulfur at the corners of an octahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur's six valence electrons each pair with a fluorine electron; the fluorines pull strongly, but the symmetric shape makes SF6 nonpolar and extremely inert.

facts: It is about 23,500 times stronger than CO2 as a greenhouse gas over 100 years.
Breathing it makes your voice sound very deep.
hazards: Non-toxic but a potent greenhouse gas.
summary: SF6 is an extremely stable insulating gas and a powerful greenhouse gas.

name: Chlorine trifluoride

bonding.summary: A T-shaped molecule: three fluorines and two lone pairs around chlorine.
bonding.electronSharing: Chlorine shares three of its seven electrons with fluorines and keeps two lone pairs, which take the equatorial positions and bend the long axial bonds slightly.

facts: It sets fire to sand, asbestos and glass, and it famously burned through a concrete floor in a 1950s spill.
summary: ClF3 is one of the most aggressive fluorinating agents known.

name: Bromine pentafluoride

bonding.summary: Five fluorines form a square pyramid; a lone pair sits under the base.
bonding.electronSharing: Bromine shares five electrons with fluorines and keeps one lone pair, which pushes the four base fluorines slightly up.

facts: Geologists use BrF5 to release oxygen from minerals to measure isotopes.
summary: BrF5 shows the square-pyramidal shape predicted by VSEPR.

name: Iodine heptafluoride

bonding.summary: Seven fluorines around iodine: two at the poles, five in a ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Iodine uses all seven valence electrons to bond to seven fluorines, the largest number of bonds of any simple main-group molecule.

facts: It is the only common example of a pentagonal bipyramidal molecule.
summary: IF7 packs seven atoms around iodine in a rare pentagonal bipyramid.

name: Titanium tetrachloride

bonding.summary: A tetrahedral molecule; unusually for a metal compound, it is a liquid.
bonding.electronSharing: Titanium shares its four valence electrons with four chlorines and has no d electrons left, so TiCl4 is colorless.

facts: It reacts with moist air to make thick white smoke, used for skywriting and smoke screens.
summary: TiCl4 is a volatile liquid on the route to titanium metal and white pigment.

name: Aluminium chloride (Al2Cl6 dimer)

structure.note: Gas-phase dimer.

bonding.summary: Two AlCl4 tetrahedra sharing an edge through two bridging chlorines.
bonding.electronSharing: Each aluminium has only six electrons in AlCl3, so a chlorine on one molecule donates a lone pair to the aluminium of the other, giving both an octet.

facts: It sublimes at 180 °C into Al2Cl6 dimers.
summary: AlCl3 pairs up into Al2Cl6 so each aluminium can complete its octet.

name: Osmium tetroxide

bonding.summary: Osmium in its +8 state with four double-bonded oxygens.
bonding.electronSharing: Osmium has given all eight valence electrons to bonds with four oxygens.

occurrence: Forms slowly when osmium powder is exposed to air.
uses: Catalyst for making diols from alkenes
facts: It is one of very few compounds with an element in the +8 oxidation state.
summary: OsO4 shows osmium in its highest oxidation state, +8.

name: Ruthenium tetroxide

bonding.summary: Ruthenium in its +8 state with four oxygens.
bonding.electronSharing: Ruthenium shares all eight valence electrons with four oxygens.

facts: It can decompose explosively above about 100 °C.
summary: RuO4 is the volatile, aggressive cousin of osmium tetroxide.

name: Xenon difluoride

bonding.summary: A linear F–Xe–F molecule; xenon keeps three lone pairs.
bonding.electronSharing: Xenon shares one electron pair across both Xe–F bonds (a three-centre four-electron bond). Its three lone pairs sit around its waist, so the molecule is straight.

facts: It can be made simply by exposing xenon and fluorine to sunlight.
summary: XeF2 proves that noble gases can form stable compounds.

name: Xenon tetrafluoride

bonding.summary: Four fluorines in a square around xenon; two lone pairs above and below.
bonding.electronSharing: Xenon shares four of its eight electrons with fluorines and keeps two lone pairs, which sit opposite each other.

facts: XeF4 was made in 1962, weeks after Bartlett's first xenon compound.
summary: XeF4 is a square-planar molecule, a textbook VSEPR example.

name: Krypton difluoride

bonding.summary: A linear molecule like XeF2, but much less stable.
bonding.electronSharing: Krypton's electrons are held more tightly than xenon's, so almost only fluorine can pull them into bonds, and then weakly.

formation: Kr + F2 -> KrF2 (electric discharge or UV at about −196 °C)
uses: One of the strongest known oxidizing and fluorinating agents, used in research
facts: KrF2 can oxidize gold to the +5 state; it decomposes slowly at room temperature.
summary: KrF2 is the main compound of krypton and a ferocious oxidizer.

name: Argon fluorohydride

bonding.summary: H–Ar covalent, Ar–F largely ionic: roughly (HAr)+ F−.
bonding.electronSharing: Argon shares a pair with hydrogen while fluorine takes most of an electron, forming an ion pair that only survives in frozen argon.

formation: HF photolysed in solid argon below −246 °C
occurrence: Made in 2000 at the University of Helsinki.
facts: It was the first neutral argon compound to be made and falls apart above about −246 °C.
summary: HArF showed that even argon can form a chemical bond.

name: Hassium tetroxide

bonding.summary: Predicted to be a tetrahedral molecule like OsO4.
bonding.electronSharing: Hassium, like osmium, appears to share all eight valence electrons with four oxygens.

formation: Hs + 2 O2 -> HsO4 (single atoms in a gas stream)
occurrence: Made one molecule at a time at GSI, Germany, in 2001.
uses: Testing the periodic table at its heaviest end
facts: Only seven HsO4 molecules were detected in the first experiment.
summary: HsO4 showed that element 108 behaves like osmium, as the periodic table predicts.

name: Chromium hexacarbonyl

bonding.summary: Six CO ligands around a chromium atom in its zero oxidation state.
bonding.electronSharing: Each CO donates its carbon lone pair to chromium, while chromium pushes d electrons back into CO's empty orbitals (back-bonding). Chromium ends up with 18 valence electrons.

uses: Catalysts and reagents in organic chemistry
facts: It obeys the 18-electron rule, like a transition-metal octet.
summary: Cr(CO)6 is a textbook example of metal–carbonyl bonding.

name: Iron pentacarbonyl

bonding.summary: Five CO ligands around iron(0) in a trigonal bipyramid.
bonding.electronSharing: Each CO donates a lone pair to iron; iron back-donates d electrons to CO. Iron reaches 18 valence electrons.

facts: It is a straw-colored liquid metal compound at room temperature.
summary: Fe(CO)5 is a liquid iron compound used to make ultrapure iron powder.

name: Nickel tetracarbonyl

bonding.summary: Four CO ligands around nickel(0) in a tetrahedron.
