bonding.electronSharing: Each CO donates a carbon lone pair to nickel, which back-donates d electrons; nickel ends with 18 electrons.

formation: Ni + 4 CO -> Ni(CO)4 (50 °C); reversed at 230 °C to deposit pure nickel (Mond process)
facts: Discovered by Ludwig Mond in 1890, it was the first binary metal carbonyl known.
summary: Ni(CO)4 lets nickel be carried away as a gas and redeposited in pure form.

name: Ferrocene

bonding.summary: An iron atom sandwiched between two flat, aromatic five-carbon rings.
bonding.electronSharing: Each C5H5− ring has six π electrons spread over all five carbons. Iron(II) bonds to the whole ring at once rather than to individual carbons, reaching 18 electrons.

uses: Building block for catalysts and materials
facts: Its 1951 discovery launched modern organometallic chemistry; the 1973 Nobel Prize honored work on its sandwich structure.
summary: Ferrocene's sandwich structure opened a new field of chemistry.

name: Cisplatin

bonding.summary: Platinum(II) at the center of a square with two Cl and two NH3 on the same side.
bonding.electronSharing: Each NH3 donates its nitrogen lone pair to platinum; the chlorides bond more ionically. In cells, the chlorides are replaced by DNA bases.

uses: Chemotherapy for testicular, ovarian, lung and other cancers
facts: Discovered as an anticancer drug by accident in 1965, when platinum electrodes stopped bacteria from dividing.
The trans isomer is not an effective drug.
summary: Cisplatin binds DNA in cancer cells and has cured most cases of testicular cancer.

name: Chloroauric acid (tetrachloroaurate ion)

structure.note: In solution: H3O+ and square-planar [AuCl4]−.

bonding.summary: Gold(III) surrounded by four chlorides in a square.
bonding.electronSharing: Gold(III) has eight d electrons and, like platinum(II), prefers four bonds in a flat square.

formation: Au + HNO3 + 4 HCl -> HAuCl4 + NO + 2 H2O (aqua regia)
occurrence: Made by dissolving gold in aqua regia.
facts: Reducing it gently makes gold nanoparticles that look ruby red, as in gold ruby glass.
summary: Chloroauric acid is what gold becomes when it dissolves in aqua regia.

name: Tetraamminecopper(II) ion

bonding.summary: Four ammonia molecules donate lone pairs to a Cu2+ ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each NH3 nitrogen gives its lone pair to empty copper orbitals, forming coordinate bonds; this changes how copper's d electrons absorb light, giving deep blue-violet.
bonding.geometry: Square planar (two water molecules bind weakly above and below)

occurrence: Forms when ammonia is added to copper salt solutions.
facts: Adding ammonia turns pale blue copper sulfate solution an intense deep blue.
summary: The deep blue copper–ammonia complex is a classic demonstration of coordinate bonding.

name: Tetraethyllead

bonding.summary: Lead bonded tetrahedrally to four ethyl groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Lead shares one pair with each ethyl carbon. The weak Pb–C bonds break easily in hot engines, releasing radicals that stop knocking.

occurrence: Synthetic; banned from road fuel worldwide by 2021. It decomposes near 200 °C before boiling.
uses: Still used in some aviation gasoline
facts: The same chemist, Thomas Midgley, introduced both leaded petrol and CFCs.
summary: Tetraethyllead made petrol engines run smoothly but spread lead pollution worldwide.

name: Carbon steel

structure.note: Carbon atoms (small, grey) sit in gaps between iron atoms; real steel also contains iron carbide grains.

bonding.summary: Iron atoms in a body-centered cubic lattice, with small carbon atoms squeezed into the gaps.
bonding.electronSharing: Iron atoms share a sea of delocalized electrons. Carbon atoms in the gaps share electrons with neighboring iron and pin the planes of atoms so they cannot slip, making steel much harder than pure iron.

formation: Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2 (blast furnace), then oxygen blowing to lower carbon to below 2%
occurrence: About 1.9 billion tonnes made each year.
facts: Steel is the most recycled material on Earth.
summary: Steel is iron hardened by a pinch of carbon: the backbone of modern construction.

name: Stainless steel (304)

structure.note: Atoms placed at random in their proportions.

bonding.summary: Iron, chromium and nickel mixed on one face-centered cubic lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: All the metal atoms share one sea of electrons. Chromium at the surface reacts with air to form an invisible, self-healing chromium-oxide film that stops rust.

formation: Melting iron with chromium and nickel in an electric arc furnace
facts: Nickel keeps 304 stainless in the face-centered cubic form, which makes it non-magnetic.
summary: Stainless steel resists rust thanks to a microscopic chromium-oxide skin.

name: Brass

structure.note: Atoms placed at random in their proportions (alpha brass).

bonding.summary: Zinc atoms substituted for some copper atoms on copper's lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Zinc's two valence electrons join copper's one-per-atom electron sea; the larger zinc atoms strain the lattice and make brass harder than copper.

facts: Brass doorknobs slowly kill bacteria on their surface.
summary: Brass is copper alloyed with zinc, golden and easy to shape.

name: Bronze

structure.note: Atoms placed at random in their proportions (about 12% tin by mass).

bonding.summary: Tin atoms dissolved in copper's lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Tin contributes four valence electrons to the shared electron sea; its large atoms block slipping planes, so bronze is much harder than either metal.

facts: Bronze gave its name to the Bronze Age.
summary: Bronze, copper hardened with tin, defined an age of human history.

name: Sterling silver

structure.note: Atom fractions; 7.5% copper by mass is about 12% of atoms.

bonding.summary: Copper atoms dissolved in silver's lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Copper and silver both give one s electron to the shared sea; smaller copper atoms strain the lattice and harden the soft silver.

formation: Melting 925 parts silver with 75 parts copper
facts: Pure silver is too soft for most uses; copper makes it durable.
summary: Sterling silver is silver toughened with copper.

name: 18-karat gold

structure.note: Atom fractions for 75% gold, 12.5% silver and 12.5% copper by mass.

bonding.summary: Gold with silver and copper atoms mixed on one lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: All three metals give one s electron each to the shared sea; the mix is harder than pure gold and the silver-to-copper ratio sets the color.

formation: Melting gold with silver and copper
facts: '18 karat' means 18 parts in 24 are gold by mass.
summary: 18k gold is three-quarters gold, hardened and tinted by silver and copper.

name: Nitinol (shape-memory alloy)

structure.note: Ordered B2 (austenite) phase; on cooling it shifts to a monoclinic martensite.

bonding.summary: An ordered compound: each Ni at the center of a cube of Ti, and vice versa.
bonding.electronSharing: Nickel and titanium share a metallic electron sea, but their ordered arrangement lets the lattice switch reversibly between two crystal forms.

formation: Melting equal numbers of nickel and titanium atoms in vacuum
occurrence: Synthetic, discovered in 1959 at the US Naval Ordnance Laboratory.
facts: Bent nitinol springs back to its remembered shape when warmed.
summary: Nitinol 'remembers' its shape because its crystal can flip between two forms.

name: Niobium-titanium superconductor

structure.note: About 47% titanium by mass.

bonding.summary: Niobium and titanium atoms mixed on a body-centered cubic lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Below about 10 K, electrons in the shared sea pair up (Cooper pairs) and flow with zero resistance.

formation: Melting niobium and titanium, then drawing into fine filaments in a copper matrix
facts: The Large Hadron Collider uses about 1,200 tonnes of NbTi superconducting cable.
summary: NbTi wire carries huge currents with zero resistance in MRI and LHC magnets.

name: Neodymium magnet

structure.note: Schematic: atoms in the right proportions; the real tetragonal cell has 68 atoms.

bonding.summary: An intermetallic compound with a complex tetragonal structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Iron's unpaired 3d electrons give strong magnetism; neodymium's 4f electrons lock that magnetism along one crystal direction so it resists being demagnetized.

formation: Melting Nd, Fe and B, then powdering, aligning in a magnetic field and sintering
facts: They are the strongest permanent magnets commercially available.
hazards: Can pinch skin; brittle and may shatter.
summary: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets, powering electric motors.

name: Samarium-cobalt magnet

bonding.summary: Samarium atoms in hexagonal channels of a cobalt framework (CaCu5 structure).
bonding.electronSharing: Cobalt's unpaired d electrons provide the magnetism; samarium's 4f electrons fix its direction along the hexagonal axis.

formation: Reducing Sm2O3 with calcium in the presence of cobalt
facts: SmCo magnets keep working above 300 °C, where neodymium magnets fail.
summary: SmCo5 is a heat-resistant permanent magnet.

name: Lanthanum nickel (hydrogen storage)

bonding.summary: La atoms in hexagonal channels of a nickel framework, with gaps that can hold hydrogen.
bonding.electronSharing: Hydrogen molecules split at the surface; the atoms slip into gaps in the lattice and share electrons with the metal, forming LaNi5H6.

facts: LaNi5 can hold hydrogen at a density higher than liquid hydrogen.
summary: LaNi5 soaks up hydrogen like a sponge, the key to NiMH batteries.

name: Terfenol-D

bonding.summary: A cubic Laves phase: Tb and Dy on a diamond-like network, Fe on linked tetrahedra.
bonding.electronSharing: Iron's d electrons and the rare earths' 4f electrons couple so strongly to the lattice that magnetizing the crystal stretches it.

formation: Melting terbium, dysprosium and iron, then growing oriented crystals
occurrence: Synthetic, developed at the US Naval Ordnance Laboratory in the 1970s.
facts: Its name stands for TERbium, FErrum (iron), Naval Ordnance Laboratory, and D for dysprosium.
summary: Terfenol-D has the largest magnetostriction of any alloy at room temperature.

name: Galinstan

structure.note: Liquid at room temperature; atoms drawn on a lattice only to show proportions.

bonding.summary: A liquid metal: gallium, indium and tin atoms sharing one electron sea with no fixed lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: The three metals share valence electrons; mixing them disrupts crystal packing so the alloy melts at about −19 °C.

formation: Melting 68.5% gallium, 21.5% indium and 10% tin by mass
uses: Non-toxic replacement for mercury in thermometers
facts: The name combines GALlium, INdium and STANnum (tin).
hazards: Low toxicity; stains skin and attacks aluminium.
summary: Galinstan is a liquid metal that replaces mercury in thermometers.

name: Pewter

structure.note: Schematic proportions; tin's real crystal is tetragonal.

bonding.summary: Mostly tin, hardened by small amounts of antimony and copper.
bonding.electronSharing: All atoms share a metallic electron sea; antimony and copper atoms disrupt slip in tin's soft lattice.

formation: Melting about 92% tin with 6% antimony and 2% copper
facts: Old pewter often contained lead, which leached into food.
summary: Pewter is a soft, low-melting tin alloy for tableware and ornaments.

name: Methane

bonding.summary: Carbon shares one pair with each of four hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon's four valence electrons pair with four hydrogen electrons; C and H pull almost equally (Δχ 0.35), so the bonds are nearly nonpolar.

formation: CO2 + 4 H2 -> CH4 + 2 H2O (also made by microbes in swamps and cows)
occurrence: Main component of natural gas; made by microbes; found on Titan and the giant planets.
facts: Methane traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years.
Titan has lakes of liquid methane and ethane.
hazards: Flammable and explosive; a potent greenhouse gas.
summary: Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and the main ingredient of natural gas.

name: Ethane

bonding.summary: Two carbons joined by a single bond, each carrying three hydrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: The C–C bond shares one pair evenly; each carbon also shares a pair with each of its three hydrogens.

occurrence: Second most common component of natural gas.
facts: The two CH3 groups spin almost freely around the C–C bond.
summary: Ethane is mostly cracked into ethylene for plastics.

name: Propane

bonding.summary: A three-carbon chain with single bonds.
bonding.electronSharing: All bonds are shared pairs between C–C and C–H with very little polarity.

formation: Separated from natural gas and oil refining
facts: Propane is stored as a liquid under modest pressure, which is why it fits in small tanks.
summary: Propane is the portable fuel in camping stoves and barbecue tanks.

name: Butane

bonding.summary: A four-carbon chain with single bonds.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs throughout, almost evenly divided between C and H.

formation: Separated from natural gas and oil refining
facts: Its isomer isobutane has the same formula but a branched shape.
summary: Butane is the liquefied fuel you see sloshing in a clear lighter.

name: Octane

bonding.summary: An eight-carbon chain; long enough that molecules stick together as a liquid.
bonding.electronSharing: All shared pairs, barely polar; van der Waals attraction between the long chains makes octane a liquid.

facts: The 'octane rating' refers to the branched isomer isooctane, not to n-octane, which knocks badly.
summary: Octane is a typical petrol molecule: a chain of eight carbons.

name: Ethylene

bonding.summary: A carbon–carbon double bond in a flat molecule.
bonding.electronSharing: The carbons share two pairs: one along the axis (σ) and one above and below the plane (π). The π bond locks the molecule flat and is easy to open, which lets ethylene join into chains.
bonding.geometry: Trigonal planar carbons, all atoms in one plane

formation: C2H6 -> C2H4 + H2 (steam cracking at about 850 °C)
occurrence: Made in larger amounts than any other organic chemical; also a plant hormone.
uses: Making polyethylene, the most common plastic
facts: A ripe banana releases ethylene that speeds up ripening of nearby fruit.
summary: Ethylene's double bond opens up to make polyethylene.

name: Acetylene

bonding.summary: A carbon–carbon triple bond in a straight line.
bonding.electronSharing: The carbons share three pairs: one σ and two π bonds at right angles. Each carbon also shares a pair with its hydrogen.

facts: An oxy-acetylene flame reaches about 3,500 °C.
At normal pressure it sublimes at −84 °C rather than melting.
summary: Acetylene's triple bond stores a lot of energy, giving the hottest common fuel flame.

name: Benzene

bonding.summary: A flat hexagonal ring with six electrons shared around the whole ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Each carbon shares pairs with two ring neighbors and one hydrogen, and gives one electron to a ring of six π electrons spread evenly over all six carbons. All C–C bonds are identical, between single and double.

formation: Catalytic reforming of naphtha from crude oil
uses: Making styrene, nylon and other plastics
facts: August Kekulé said the ring structure came to him in a dream of a snake biting its own tail.
summary: Benzene's ring of shared electrons is the prototype of aromatic chemistry.

name: Naphthalene

bonding.summary: Two benzene rings fused along one edge.
bonding.electronSharing: Ten π electrons are delocalized over both rings.

occurrence: Coal tar and crude oil; detected in interstellar space.
facts: It sublimes slowly at room temperature, which is why mothballs shrink.
summary: Naphthalene is two benzene rings fused together.

name: Cyclohexane

bonding.summary: A ring of six carbons with single bonds only.
bonding.electronSharing: Only single shared pairs, so the ring puckers into a 'chair' that keeps every bond angle near the ideal 109.5°.

facts: Its chair shape is free of strain, unlike flat rings.
summary: Cyclohexane shows how rings of single bonds pucker into chairs.

name: Methanol

bonding.summary: A methyl group attached to an OH group.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen pulls electrons from both carbon and hydrogen; the polar O–H lets methanol hydrogen-bond like water.

occurrence: Made from natural gas; found in interstellar clouds.
facts: As little as 10 mL of methanol can cause blindness.
summary: Methanol is the simplest alcohol and a key industrial chemical.

name: Ethanol

bonding.summary: An ethyl group attached to an OH group.
bonding.electronSharing: The polar O–H group hydrogen-bonds with water, so ethanol mixes with water completely; the ethyl part dissolves oils.

facts: A cloud near the center of the Milky Way contains enough ethanol for billions of billions of drinks.
hazards: Flammable; intoxicating and toxic in excess.
summary: Ethanol is made by yeast and used in drinks, fuels and disinfectants.

name: Glycerol

bonding.summary: A three-carbon chain with an OH on each carbon.
bonding.electronSharing: Three O–H groups hydrogen-bond strongly, making glycerol thick, sweet and water-loving.

occurrence: The backbone of fats and oils.
facts: Every molecule of fat is glycerol joined to three fatty acids.
summary: Glycerol is the backbone of fats, sweet and syrupy.

name: Ethylene glycol

bonding.summary: Two carbons each carrying an OH group.
bonding.electronSharing: Its two O–H groups hydrogen-bond with water, disrupting ice formation.

uses: Making PET plastic bottles and polyester
facts: A 50:50 mix with water freezes only at about −37 °C.
hazards: Toxic if swallowed, despite its sweet taste.
summary: Ethylene glycol keeps engines from freezing and makes PET plastic.

name: Phenol

bonding.summary: An OH group attached to a benzene ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen's lone pair partly joins the ring's π electrons, which makes the O–H more acidic than in alcohols.

facts: Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery in 1867 using carbolic acid.
summary: Phenol launched antiseptic surgery and is a key plastics feedstock.

name: Acetone

bonding.summary: A C=O group flanked by two methyl groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen pulls the two shared pairs of the C=O bond toward itself, making acetone polar and a good solvent.

formation: Co-product of the cumene process (with phenol)
occurrence: Synthetic; small amounts made in the body.
facts: The body makes acetone when burning fat, and it can be smelled on the breath during fasting.
summary: Acetone is the simplest ketone and a powerful solvent.

name: Acetic acid

bonding.summary: A methyl group attached to a carboxyl group, COOH.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=O pulls electrons from the O–H, letting it release H+; the resulting acetate ion spreads the negative charge over both oxygens.

uses: Making vinyl acetate for paints and glues
facts: Pure acetic acid freezes at 16.6 °C, forming ice-like crystals: 'glacial' acetic acid.
summary: Acetic acid gives vinegar its sour taste.

name: Formic acid

bonding.summary: The simplest carboxylic acid: H attached to COOH.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=O pulls electrons from the O–H, so it releases H+ fairly easily.

facts: Its name comes from Latin formica, ant, because it was first distilled from ants.
summary: Formic acid is the sting in ant bites.

name: Urea

bonding.summary: A C=O group flanked by two NH2 groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Nitrogen lone pairs partly join the C=O π bond, making the molecule flat and very polar.

occurrence: Urine; made industrially in huge amounts.
facts: Friedrich Wöhler's 1828 synthesis of urea from inorganic salts helped end the belief that living things contain a special 'vital force'.
summary: Wöhler's 1828 urea synthesis was a famous early case of making an organic compound from inorganic starting materials.

name: Chloroform

bonding.summary: Carbon bonded to one hydrogen and three chlorines.
bonding.electronSharing: The three chlorines pull electrons from carbon, making the C–H slightly acidic and the molecule polar.

occurrence: Synthetic; small amounts made by seaweed.
facts: It was a common surgical anesthetic in the 1800s, used for Queen Victoria in childbirth.
summary: Chloroform was an early anesthetic and is now a solvent and chemical feedstock.

name: Carbon tetrachloride

bonding.summary: Carbon bonded to four chlorines in a tetrahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Each C–Cl bond is polar, but the four pull equally in symmetric directions, so CCl4 is nonpolar.

uses: Formerly fire extinguishers, dry cleaning and refrigerant production (now restricted)
facts: It is a classic example of polar bonds in a nonpolar molecule.
summary: CCl4 shows how symmetry cancels bond polarity.

name: Vinyl chloride (PVC monomer)

bonding.summary: Ethylene with one hydrogen replaced by chlorine.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=C double bond opens up during polymerization to link thousands of units into PVC chains.

uses: Making PVC pipes, window frames and cable insulation
facts: PVC is the third most produced plastic.
summary: Vinyl chloride is the building block of PVC.

name: Styrene (polystyrene monomer)

bonding.summary: A vinyl group (C=C) attached to a benzene ring.
bonding.electronSharing: The vinyl double bond is conjugated with the ring's π electrons; it opens to form polystyrene chains.

facts: Expanded polystyrene foam is about 98% air.
summary: Styrene links up to make polystyrene.

name: Tetrafluoroethylene (Teflon monomer)

bonding.summary: Ethylene with all four hydrogens replaced by fluorine.
bonding.electronSharing: The strong, polar C–F bonds wrap the carbon chain in fluorine, which makes the polymer (PTFE) slippery and inert.

uses: Making PTFE (Teflon) for non-stick pans, seals and cables
facts: PTFE was discovered by accident in 1938 when a cylinder of TFE gas turned into white powder.
summary: TFE polymerizes into Teflon, one of the most slippery solids.

name: Diethyl ether

bonding.summary: An oxygen atom linking two ethyl groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen shares a pair with each carbon and keeps two lone pairs; with no O–H, ether cannot hydrogen-bond to itself, so it boils at only 34.6 °C.

facts: The first public demonstration of ether anesthesia was in Boston in 1846.
summary: Diethyl ether made painless surgery possible.

name: Nitroglycerin

bonding.summary: Glycerol with three nitrate groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Fuel (C and H) and oxidizer (nitrate oxygen) sit in the same molecule, so it can rearrange explosively into N2, CO2 and water.
bonding.geometry: Flexible chain with planar NO2 groups

uses: Heart medicine for angina (relaxes blood vessels)
facts: Alfred Nobel tamed it into dynamite and later funded the Nobel Prizes; decades later nitroglycerin was prescribed for his own heart condition.
summary: Nitroglycerin is both a powerful explosive and a heart medicine.

name: Trinitrotoluene (TNT)

bonding.summary: A toluene ring carrying three nitro groups.
bonding.electronSharing: The nitro groups pull electrons from the ring; the molecule stores oxygen and fuel together but is stable enough to melt and pour.
bonding.geometry: Planar ring with twisted NO2 groups

formation: Toluene + 3 HNO3 -> TNT + 3 H2O (with sulfuric acid)
uses: Standard unit of explosive energy (tons of TNT)
facts: Its stability made it safe enough to melt and pour into shells.
summary: TNT is the reference explosive used to measure explosive energy.

name: Glucose

bonding.summary: A six-membered ring of five carbons and one oxygen, with OH groups around it.
bonding.electronSharing: All bonds are shared pairs; the five O–H groups make glucose very soluble in water through hydrogen bonds.

occurrence: Blood, fruit, honey; made by every green plant.
facts: Your brain burns about 120 g of glucose a day.
summary: Glucose is the fuel that photosynthesis makes and almost all cells burn.

name: Fructose

bonding.summary: Same atoms as glucose, arranged with a ketone group instead of an aldehyde.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs throughout; many OH groups hydrogen-bond to water.
bonding.geometry: Five- or six-membered ring in solution

facts: Fructose is the sweetest natural sugar, about 1.7 times as sweet as table sugar.
summary: Fructose is glucose's sweeter twin with the same formula.

name: Sucrose

bonding.summary: A glucose ring and a fructose ring joined through an oxygen bridge.
bonding.electronSharing: The glycosidic C–O–C link shares electrons between the two sugar rings; eight OH groups hydrogen-bond strongly.

facts: Sugar crystals give off flashes of light when crushed (triboluminescence).
hazards: Harmless; excess harms teeth and health.
summary: Table sugar is glucose and fructose joined together.

name: Ribose

bonding.summary: A five-carbon sugar, the backbone sugar of RNA.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs with polar O–H groups.

formation: Made in cells by the pentose phosphate pathway
facts: Ribose was found in meteorites in 2019.
summary: Ribose is the 'R' in RNA.

name: Deoxyribose

bonding.summary: Ribose missing one oxygen at carbon 2.
bonding.electronSharing: Lacking the 2′-OH group makes DNA much more chemically stable than RNA.

facts: 'Deoxy' means 'missing an oxygen'.
summary: Deoxyribose is the 'D' in DNA.

name: Glycine

bonding.summary: The simplest amino acid: an amino group and an acid group on one carbon.
bonding.electronSharing: In water the acid gives its H+ to the amino group, making a zwitterion with + and − ends.

formation: Made in the body from serine; found in comets
occurrence: In proteins; detected in comet 67P by Rosetta.
facts: Glycine was found in samples from comet Wild 2 returned by NASA's Stardust mission.
summary: Glycine is the smallest amino acid and has been found in comets.

name: Alanine

bonding.summary: Glycine with a methyl side chain.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs; the central carbon has four different groups, so alanine has left- and right-handed forms.

facts: Life uses almost only the L-form; meteorites contain both forms.
summary: Alanine is the simplest chiral amino acid.

name: Cysteine

bonding.summary: An amino acid with an SH (thiol) side chain.
bonding.electronSharing: Two cysteines can each give up an H and share electrons in an S–S bond, a disulfide bridge that holds proteins in shape.

formation: Made from serine and methionine in the body
occurrence: Proteins, especially hair and skin keratin.
facts: Perms work by breaking and re-forming disulfide bonds in hair.
summary: Cysteine's sulfur forms the disulfide bridges that shape proteins.

name: Tryptophan

bonding.summary: An amino acid with a large indole ring side chain.
bonding.electronSharing: The indole ring's ten π electrons are delocalized; it absorbs UV light, which is how proteins are measured.

facts: Turkey has no more tryptophan than most protein foods, so it is not why you feel sleepy after a holiday meal.
summary: Tryptophan is the body's raw material for serotonin.

name: Adenine

bonding.summary: A double ring (purine) of carbon and nitrogen.
bonding.electronSharing: π electrons are shared over both rings. Adenine pairs with thymine (or uracil) through two hydrogen bonds.

occurrence: DNA, RNA, ATP; found in meteorites.
uses: Part of ATP, NAD and coenzyme A
facts: Adenine is literally a pentamer of HCN: five HCN units have the same atoms.
summary: Adenine is the 'A' in DNA and the core of the energy molecule ATP.

name: Guanine

bonding.summary: A purine with a C=O and an NH2 group.
bonding.electronSharing: Delocalized π electrons over both rings; guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds.

formation: Made in cells from simpler molecules
uses: Pearly shimmer in cosmetics (from fish scales)
facts: Guanine crystals make fish scales and spider bodies shimmer.
summary: Guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds.

name: Cytosine

bonding.summary: A single ring (pyrimidine) with C=O and NH2.
bonding.electronSharing: π electrons spread over the ring; three hydrogen bonds join it to guanine.

facts: Adding a methyl group to cytosine switches genes off (epigenetics).
summary: Cytosine is the 'C' of the genetic code.

name: Thymine

bonding.summary: A pyrimidine ring with two C=O groups and a methyl.
bonding.electronSharing: Two hydrogen bonds join thymine to adenine.

formation: Made from uracil by adding a methyl group
occurrence: Mainly DNA; small amounts in tRNA as ribothymidine.
facts: UV light can fuse neighboring thymines in DNA, a main cause of sunburn damage.
summary: Thymine is DNA's version of uracil.

name: Uracil

bonding.summary: A pyrimidine ring with two C=O groups.
bonding.electronSharing: Pairs with adenine through two hydrogen bonds in RNA.

occurrence: RNA; found in meteorites and in samples from asteroid Ryugu.
uses: Genetic code letter U in RNA
facts: Uracil was detected in samples brought back from asteroid Ryugu.
summary: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

name: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)

bonding.summary: Adenine and ribose attached to a chain of three phosphate groups.
bonding.electronSharing: The phosphate groups crowd negative charges together; breaking off the last phosphate releases energy that cells use.
bonding.geometry: Purine ring, ribose ring and a phosphate chain

formation: ADP + phosphate -> ATP + H2O (ATP synthase, driven by respiration)
facts: You recycle roughly your own body weight in ATP every day.
summary: ATP is the universal energy currency of life.

name: Cholesterol

bonding.summary: Four fused rings (a steroid) with a small OH group and a hydrocarbon tail.
bonding.electronSharing: Almost all bonds are nonpolar C–C and C–H, so cholesterol is oily; the single OH lets it sit in cell membranes.

formation: Made in the liver from acetyl-CoA (over 30 steps)
uses: Raw material for steroid hormones, vitamin D and bile acids
facts: Its structure, worked out partly by Heinrich Wieland and Adolf Windaus, earned Nobel Prizes in 1927 and 1928.
hazards: High blood levels raise heart-disease risk.
summary: Cholesterol stiffens membranes and is the parent of steroid hormones.

name: Palmitic acid

bonding.summary: A straight 16-carbon saturated chain ending in COOH.
bonding.electronSharing: The long nonpolar tail avoids water while the acid head is polar: the basis of soaps and membranes.

formation: Made by fatty acid synthase from acetyl-CoA
facts: It is the most common saturated fat in animals and plants.
summary: Palmitic acid is the most common saturated fatty acid.

name: Oleic acid

bonding.summary: An 18-carbon chain with one cis double bond in the middle.
bonding.electronSharing: The cis C=C puts a kink in the chain, so molecules cannot pack tightly; that keeps olive oil liquid.

facts: Its trans twin, elaidic acid, is a solid trans fat.
summary: Oleic acid's kink keeps olive oil liquid.

name: Heme B

structure.source: Flat 2D layout from PubChem (CID 4973); no 3D model exists for this molecule

bonding.summary: An iron ion held at the center of a flat porphyrin ring by four nitrogens.
bonding.electronSharing: The porphyrin's 18-electron aromatic ring donates four nitrogen lone pairs to iron. Iron uses a fifth and sixth position to bind the protein and O2.
bonding.geometry: Flat porphyrin with Fe in the center

formation: Made from glycine and succinyl-CoA in eight steps
facts: Each red blood cell holds about 270 million hemoglobin molecules, each with four hemes.
summary: Heme's iron grabs oxygen in your blood and makes it red.

name: Chlorophyll a

structure.source: Flat 2D layout from PubChem (CID 12085802); no 3D model exists for this molecule

bonding.summary: A magnesium ion at the center of a flat ring, with a long oily tail.
bonding.electronSharing: Four nitrogen lone pairs hold Mg2+. Delocalized π electrons over the ring absorb red and blue light and pass the energy on, which is why leaves look green.
bonding.geometry: Flat chlorin ring with a phytol tail

formation: Made in plants from glutamate in many steps
facts: Chlorophyll and heme are built on very similar rings, one around magnesium, one around iron.
summary: Chlorophyll captures sunlight to power almost all life on Earth.

name: Thyroxine (T4)

bonding.summary: Two iodinated benzene rings joined by an oxygen, with an amino-acid tail.
bonding.electronSharing: Four large iodine atoms bond to the rings; the shape fits the thyroid hormone receptor.

formation: Made in the thyroid from tyrosine and iodine
facts: About 65% of thyroxine's mass is iodine.
summary: Thyroxine is the iodine-rich hormone that sets your metabolic rate.

name: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)

bonding.summary: A five-membered lactone ring with an enediol group.
bonding.electronSharing: The enediol group gives up electrons easily, which makes vitamin C an antioxidant.
bonding.geometry: Planar ring with a side chain

formation: Made from glucose in most animals, but not in humans
facts: Scurvy killed more sailors than battles until citrus was added to rations.
summary: Vitamin C is an antioxidant humans must get from food.

name: Retinol (vitamin A)

bonding.summary: A ring and a chain of alternating single and double bonds.
bonding.electronSharing: Five conjugated C=C bonds share π electrons along the chain. In the eye, light flips one double bond from cis to trans, triggering vision.

occurrence: Liver, eggs, dairy; made from beta-carotene.
facts: Vision starts when one photon flips a cis double bond in retinal to trans.
summary: Vitamin A's conjugated chain is the light switch of vision.

name: Beta-carotene

bonding.summary: A long chain of eleven conjugated double bonds between two rings.
bonding.electronSharing: π electrons spread along the whole chain absorb blue light, so carrots look orange.

formation: Made in plants from isoprene units
facts: Eating huge amounts of carrots can turn your skin orange (carotenemia).
summary: Beta-carotene's long chain of shared electrons makes carrots orange.

name: Lactic acid

bonding.summary: A three-carbon acid with an OH next to the acid group.
bonding.electronSharing: The COOH releases H+; the OH and acid group hydrogen-bond.

formation: Pyruvate + NADH + H+ -> lactate + NAD+ (fermentation in muscles and bacteria)
facts: Lactic acid is not what makes muscles sore the next day; it is cleared within an hour.
summary: Lactic acid makes yogurt tangy and is turned into compostable plastic.

name: Citric acid

bonding.summary: Three carboxylic acid groups and one OH on a five-carbon frame.
bonding.electronSharing: Three acid groups release H+ in steps; together they grab metal ions (chelation).

formation: Made by Aspergillus niger mold from sugar
occurrence: Citrus fruit; every cell's citric acid cycle.
facts: Its role in metabolism, the citric acid (Krebs) cycle, earned Hans Krebs the 1953 Nobel Prize.
summary: Citric acid gives lemons their sourness and sits at the hub of metabolism.

name: Dopamine

bonding.summary: A benzene ring with two OH groups and an aminoethyl tail.
bonding.electronSharing: The catechol (two OH) ring and the amine let it fit receptor proteins in the brain.

uses: Neurotransmitter for movement, motivation and reward
facts: Parkinson's disease involves the loss of dopamine-making neurons; L-DOPA helps replace it.
summary: Dopamine is a brain messenger for movement and reward.

name: Serotonin

bonding.summary: An indole ring with an OH group and an aminoethyl chain.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs and a delocalized indole ring; the amine is positively charged in the body.

uses: Neurotransmitter for mood, sleep and digestion
facts: Most of your serotonin is in your gut, not your brain.
summary: Serotonin regulates mood, sleep and digestion.

name: Adrenaline (epinephrine)

bonding.summary: Like dopamine with an extra OH and a methyl on the nitrogen.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs; the catechol ring and amine bind adrenergic receptors.

formation: Noradrenaline -> adrenaline (adding a methyl in the adrenal gland)
facts: It was the first hormone isolated and synthesized, around 1900–1904.
summary: Adrenaline powers the fight-or-flight response.

name: Caffeine

bonding.summary: A purine double ring with three methyl groups and two C=O.
bonding.electronSharing: π electrons are shared over the rings; its shape mimics adenosine, so it blocks adenosine receptors that signal tiredness.

formation: Made in coffee and tea plants from xanthosine
uses: Medicine for apnea in premature babies
facts: Plants make caffeine partly as a natural insecticide.
hazards: High doses cause jitters and heart rhythm problems.
summary: Caffeine keeps you alert by blocking the brain's 'tired' signal.

name: Nicotine

bonding.summary: A pyridine ring linked to a pyrrolidine ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Nitrogen lone pairs let nicotine bind acetylcholine receptors in nerves and muscle.

facts: It is one of the most addictive substances known.
summary: Nicotine mimics a natural nerve signal, which makes tobacco so addictive.

name: Aspirin

bonding.summary: A benzene ring with an acid group and an ester group side by side.
bonding.electronSharing: The acetyl group transfers to the COX enzyme, permanently blocking it and reducing prostaglandins that cause pain and inflammation.

formation: Salicylic acid + acetic anhydride -> aspirin + acetic acid
uses: Preventing heart attacks and strokes (low dose)
facts: People chewed willow bark, which contains salicin, for pain for thousands of years.
hazards: Stomach bleeding; not for children (Reye's syndrome).
summary: Aspirin is one of the oldest and most used synthetic medicines.

name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen)

bonding.summary: A benzene ring with an OH and an amide group on opposite sides.
bonding.electronSharing: Shared pairs throughout; the amide nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the C=O.

facts: Even after over a century of use, exactly how it works is still debated.
summary: Paracetamol is a common painkiller that is safe at normal doses but dangerous in overdose.

name: Ibuprofen

bonding.summary: A benzene ring with an isobutyl group and a propanoic acid group.
bonding.electronSharing: The acid group and greasy side chains let it sit in the COX enzyme's channel and block it reversibly.
bonding.geometry: Chiral center next to the ring

facts: It was first tested by its co-inventor on his own hangover.
hazards: Stomach irritation; kidney effects in overdose.
summary: Ibuprofen is a widely used anti-inflammatory painkiller.

name: Penicillin G

bonding.summary: A strained four-membered beta-lactam ring fused to a sulfur-containing ring.
bonding.electronSharing: The strained beta-lactam ring snaps open and bonds to the bacterial enzyme that builds cell walls, disabling it.

uses: Antibiotic for strep, syphilis and other infections
facts: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a forgotten culture plate.
summary: Penicillin, the first true antibiotic, kills bacteria by wrecking their cell walls.

name: Morphine

bonding.summary: A rigid five-ring framework with one aromatic ring.
bonding.electronSharing: The amine nitrogen and phenol OH let morphine bind opioid receptors, mimicking the body's endorphins.

facts: It was the first alkaloid isolated from a plant, by Friedrich Sertürner in 1804.
summary: Morphine is a powerful painkiller with serious risks.

name: Capsaicin

bonding.summary: A vanillyl ring linked by an amide to a fatty chain.
bonding.electronSharing: Its oily tail makes it dissolve in fats rather than water, which is why milk soothes better than water.

facts: It triggers the same nerve receptor (TRPV1) that senses painful heat.
summary: Capsaicin tricks heat-sensing nerves, making chilies taste hot.

name: Menthol

bonding.summary: A cyclohexane ring with an OH, a methyl and an isopropyl group.
bonding.electronSharing: Mostly nonpolar bonds with one polar OH; it activates cold-sensing nerve receptors.

formation: Extracted from mint oil or made from thymol
facts: It triggers TRPM8, the same receptor that senses cold.
summary: Menthol feels cold by switching on cold-sensing nerves.

name: Vanillin

bonding.summary: A benzene ring with aldehyde, methoxy and OH groups.
bonding.electronSharing: The aldehyde and phenol groups are conjugated with the ring, giving a strong scent.

formation: Made from guaiacol or lignin; natural vanillin from cured vanilla pods
facts: Less than 1% of vanilla flavoring comes from real vanilla beans.
summary: Vanillin is the main flavor molecule of vanilla.
